<!-- defi-1: body_md -->
A covering map of compact metric spaces $f\colon\mathcal{M}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$ is
\emph{locally expanding} if there exist constants $\delta>0$ and $L>1$ such
that
\[
d(f(x), f(y))\ge Ld(x,y)
\]
whenever $x,y\in\mathcal{M}$ satisfy $d(x,y)<\delta$.
<!-- end defi-1 -->
<!-- defi-2: body_md -->
\label{def:locallyexpanding}
Let $f\colon\mathcal{M}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$ be a covering map of a compact space $\mathcal{M}$. We say that
$f$ is \emph{locally expanding} if it generates an expansive action of the
monoid generated by $f$: that is, if there exists a neighborhood of the
diagonal, or \emph{entourage}, $U\subset\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{M}$ such that
\[
(f^n(x),f^n(y))\in U \quad\text{for all } n\ge 0
\]
implies $x=y$.
<!-- end defi-2 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{theorem1}
The Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension of the limit space of $G$ is equal to $\inf\{p\colon\theta_p<1\}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{th:gradientalgebras}
The Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension of $\mathcal{M}$ is equal to the infimum of
all $p$ for which $\mathcal{D}_p$ is dense in $C(\mathcal{M})$. Moreover, if $p$ is
larger than the Ahlfors-regular conformal dimension, then the infimum of all
$\lambda$ for which $\mathcal{D}_{p,\lambda}$ is dense in $C(\mathcal{M})$ is equal
to $\theta_p$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- defi-3: body_md -->
A \emph{self-similar group} is a pair $(G, \mathfrak{B})$, where $G$ is a discrete group, and $\mathfrak{B}$ is a set together with commuting left and right actions of $G$ on it (such sets are called $G$-\emph{bisets}), such that the right action is free and has finitely many orbits. Here an action $(x, g)\mapsto x\cdot g$ for $x\in\mathfrak{B}$ and $g\in G$ is said to be free if $x\cdot g=x$ implies $g=1$.

    Two self-similar groups $(G_i, \mathfrak{B}_i)$, for $i=1, 2$, are called \emph{equivalent} if there exists an isomorphism $\phi\colon G_1\longrightarrow G_2$ of groups and a bijection $F\colon\mathfrak{B}_1\longrightarrow\mathfrak{B}_2$ such that $F(g_1\cdot x\cdot g_2)=\phi(g_1)\cdot F(x)\cdot\phi(g_2)$ for all $g_1, g_2\in G_1$ and $x\in\mathfrak{B}_1$.
<!-- end defi-3 -->
<!-- defi-4: body_md -->
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a self-similar group. A \emph{basis} of $\mathfrak{B}$ is a set $\mathsf{X}\subset\mathfrak{B}$ intersecting every orbit of the right action of $G$ on $\mathfrak{B}$ exactly once.
<!-- end defi-4 -->
<!-- defi-5: body_md -->
A \emph{topological virtual endomorphism} is a pair of continuous maps $f, \iota\colon\mathcal{M}_1\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$, where $\mathcal{M}_1, \mathcal{M}$ are path-connected topological spaces, and $f$ is a finite degree covering map.
<!-- end defi-5 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:angledoubling}
Consider the angle doubling map $f\colon\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ given by $f(x)=2x$, seen as a topological virtual endomorphism with $\iota$ equal to the identity map. Choose $t=0$ as the basepoint. We have $f^{-1}(0)=\{0, 1/2\}$. The biset $\mathfrak{B}_f$ consists of pairs $(z, [\alpha])$, where $z\in\{0, 1/2\}$, and $\alpha$ is a homotopy class of a path from $0$ to $z$. Since $z$ is uniquely determined by $\alpha$, we omit it. The homotopy class $[\alpha]$ is determined by the winding number $m\in\frac 12\mathbb{Z}$. Namely, a winding number $m$ corresponds to the homotopy class of the image in $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ of a path from $0$ to $m$ in $\mathbb{R}$. Similarly, the fundamental group of $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ is naturally identified with $\mathbb{Z}$. We get the following actions of $\mathbb{Z}=\pi_1(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$ on $\mathfrak{B}_f$:
\[[m]\cdot [n]=[m+n],\qquad [n]\cdot [m]=\left[\frac n2+m\right],\]
where $[m]\in\mathfrak{B}_f$ and $[n]\in\pi_1(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$ are elements associated with the corresponding numbers $m\in\frac 12\mathbb{Z}$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.

We usually denote the elements $[0], [1/2]$ of $\mathfrak{B}_f$ by $0$ and $1$, respectively. Then, for the generator $a=[1]$ of $\pi_1(\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z})$, we get the recurrent formulae
\[a\cdot 0=1,\qquad a\cdot 1=0\cdot a,\]
i.e., by the wreath recursion
\[a=(01)(1, a).\]
It follows that, in this notation, $a(x_0x_1\ldots x_{n-1})=y_0y_1\ldots y_{n-1}$ if and only if $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}y_i2^i=1+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_i2^i\pmod{2^n}$, i.e., $a$ acts as adding 1 to an integer written in base 2.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:basilicaimgcomput}
Consider the polynomial $f(z)=z^2-1$. Denote $\mathcal{M}_0=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0, -1\}$, and $\mathcal{M}_1=f^{-1}(\mathcal{M}_0)=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0, 1, -1\}$. Consider the topological virtual endomorphism \[f, \iota\colon \mathcal{M}_1\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}_0,\]
where $\iota$ is the identity embedding.

\begin{figure}
    \centering
    \includegraphics{basilicaab.eps}
    \caption{Generators of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$}
    \label{fig:basilicaab}
\end{figure}

The fundamental group of $\mathcal{M}_0$ is generated by loops $a$ and $b$ going around $-1$ and $0$, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:basilicaab}. We choose the fixed point $t=\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}2$ as the basepoint for the fundamental group. We have $f^{-1}(t)=\{t, -t\}$.

Consider the elements $x_0$ and $x_1$ of $\mathfrak{B}_{f, \iota}$ defined by the path from $t$ to $-t$ shown in Figure~\ref{fig:basilicaimg} and the trivial path at $t$, respectively.

\begin{figure}
    \centering 
    \includegraphics{basilicaimg.eps}
    \caption{Computation of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$}
    \label{fig:basilicaimg}
\end{figure}

We have the following relations in $\mathfrak{B}_{f, \iota}$. We replace here $x_0, x_1$ by $0$ and $1$, respectively.
\begin{alignat*}{2}
a\cdot 0&=1,&\qquad a\cdot 1&=0\cdot b,\\
b\cdot 0&=0,&\qquad b\cdot 1&=1\cdot a.
\end{alignat*}
Equivalently, $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$ is generated by the wreath recursion
\[a=(01)(1, b),\qquad b=(1, a).\]
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- defi-6: body_md -->
We say that a self-similar group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is \emph{contracting} if there exists a finite set $\mathcal{N}\subset G$ such that for every $g\in G$ there exists $n\ge 0$ such that $g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ of length at least $n$.

    The smallest set $\mathcal{N}$ satisfying this condition is called the \emph{nucleus} of the group (with respect to the basis $\mathsf{X}$).
<!-- end defi-6 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
Let $a$ be the generator of the iterated monodromy group of the angle-doubling map, see Example~\ref{ex:angledoubling}. Then, we have
\[a^2|_1=a^2|_0=a.\]
Consequently, by~\eqref{eq:sections}, for every element $g$ of the iterated monodromy group there exists $n$ such that $g|_v\in\{1, a, a^{-1}\}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ of length at least $n$. It follows that the group is contracting with the nucleus $\mathcal{N}=\{1, a, a^{-1}\}$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:basilicanucleus}
Consider the group $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$ from Example~\ref{ex:basilicaimgcomput}. We have 
\begin{alignat*}{2}
a^2&=(b, b), &\quad b^2&=(1, a^2),\\
ab&=(01)(1, ba), &\quad ba&=(01)(a, b),\\
ab^{-1}&=(01)(1, ba^{-1}),&\quad a^{-1}b&=(01)(b^{-1}, a).
\end{alignat*}
These equalities imply that the nucleus of this group is $\{1, a, a^{-1}, b, b^{-1}, ab^{-1}, ba^{-1}\}$.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{pr:sumgeometric}
    Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a self-similar group. Choose a basis $\mathsf{X}\subset\mathfrak{B}$. Suppose $G$ is contracting with respect to $\mathsf{X}$. Then for every finite set $A\subset\mathfrak{B}$ there exists a finite set $\mathcal{N}_A\subset G$ such that every product $a_1\otimes a_2\otimes\cdots\otimes a_n$ of elements of $A$ is equal to $v\cdot g$ for $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ and $g\in\mathcal{N}_A$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
If $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is contracting with respect to one basis, then it is contracting with respect to any basis.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
If $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is contracting, then its self-similarity complex is Gromov hyperbolic.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\begin{figure}
    \centering 
    \includegraphics{admcom.eps}
    \caption{The self-similarity complex for the odometer}
    \label{fig:admcom}
\end{figure}
See Figure~\ref{fig:admcom}, where a part of the self-similarity complex for the adding machine action of $\mathbb{Z}$ from Example~\ref{ex:angledoubling} is shown.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{pr:lims}
Every point of $\mathcal{J}_{(G, \mathfrak{B})}$ is the limit $\lambda(\ldots x_2x_1)$ of a sequence $\emptyset, x_1, x_2x_1, x_3x_2x_1, \ldots$ for some $\ldots x_2x_1\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$. The map $\lambda\colon\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}\longrightarrow\mathcal{J}_{(G, \mathfrak{B})}$ is a quotient map. We have $\lambda(\ldots x_2x_1)=\lambda(\ldots y_2y_1)$ if and only if there exists a finite set $N\subset G$ and a sequence $g_n\in N$ (equivalently, a sequence $g_n\in\mathcal{N}$, where $\mathcal{N}$ is the nucleus) such that $g_n(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)=y_n\ldots y_2y_1$ for every $n$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{ex:realcircle}
Consider the adding machine from Example~\ref{ex:angledoubling}. Denote, for $w=\ldots x_2x_1\in\{0, 1\}^{-\omega}$ by $\theta(w)$ the point of $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ represented by the real number $\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k2^{-k}$, i.e., by the binary real $.x_1x_2\ldots$. If $a^{n_k}$ is a sequence such that $a^{n_k}(x_k\ldots x_1)=y_k\ldots y_1$, then $|\theta(\ldots x_2x_1)-\theta(\ldots y_2y_1)|\le 2^{-k}n_k$. Consequently, if the sequence $(n_k)$ is bounded, then $\theta(\ldots x_2x_1)=\theta(\ldots y_2y_1)$. 

Conversely, if $\theta(w_1)=\theta(w_2)$, then the sequences $w_i$ are of the form $\ldots 0001x_n\ldots x_2x_1$ and $\ldots 1110x_n\ldots x_2x_1$. We have
\[a(111\ldots 10x_n\ldots x_2x_1)=000\ldots 01x_n\ldots x_2x_1,\]
hence $w_1$ and $w_2$ are equivalent (represent the same point of the limit space).

It follows that the  limit space in this case is homeomorphic to the circle $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ and the limit dynamical system is the angle doubling map.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{th:limstheorem}
    Let $f\colon\mathcal{M}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$ be a locally expanding covering map, where $\mathcal{M}$ is a compact metric space. Then the limit dynamical system of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(f)$ is topologically conjugate to $f$. In particular, the limit space of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(f)$ is homeomorphic to $\mathcal{M}$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- defi-7: body_md -->
Consider the topological space $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}\times G$, where $G$ is discrete. We say that $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g, \ldots y_2y_1\cdot h\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}\times G$ are \emph{asymptotically equivalent} if there exists a finite set $N\subset G$ and a sequence $g_n\in N$ such that
    \[g_n\cdot x_n\ldots x_2x_1\cdot g=y_n\ldots y_2y_1\cdot h\]
    for all $n$. 

    The quotient of $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}\times G$ by the asymptotic equivalence relation is denoted $\mathcal{X}_{G}=\mathcal{X}_{(G, \mathfrak{B})}$, and is called the \emph{limit $G$-space}. The right action of $G$ on $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ is induced by the natural right action of $G$ on $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}\times G$.
<!-- end defi-7 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
Similar arguments to those in Example~\ref{ex:realcircle} show that the limit $G$-space of the binary adding machine is naturally homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual action of $\mathbb{Z}$ on it. The image of a sequence $\ldots x_2x_1\cdot a^n\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}\times G$ is the real number $n+\sum_{k=1}^\infty x_k2^{-k}$.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- defi-8: body_md -->
\label{def:regularssgroup}
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a self-similar group, and let $\mathsf{X}\subset\mathfrak{B}$ be a basis. We say that $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is \emph{regular} if for every $x_1x_2\ldots\in\mathsf{X}^\omega$ there exists $n$ such that $g(x_1x_2\ldots x_n)\ne x_1x_2\ldots x_n$ or $g|_{x_1x_2\ldots x_n}=1$. (This is equivalent to the condition that the groupoid of germs of the action of $G$ on $\mathsf{X}^\omega$ is \emph{principal}, i.e., that all its isotropy groups are trivial.)
<!-- end defi-8 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{th:regularimg}
    The action of $G$ on $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ is free if and only if $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is regular. 

    A self-similar contracting group is regular if and only if it is equivalent to the iterated monodromy group of a locally expanding covering map $f\colon\mathcal{M}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$.

The limit dynamical system of the iterated monodromy group of a locally expanding covering map $f\colon\mathcal{M}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}$ is topologically conjugate to $f$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:intersectingtiles}
Let $v, u\in\mathsf{X}^*$ be such that $|v|\ge |u|$. Then the tiles $\mathcal{T}_v, \mathcal{T}_u$ intersect if and only if there exists $g\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $u$ is a suffix of $g(v)$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $v=v_1u_1$, where $|u_1|=|u|$. Suppose that $g(v_1u_1)$ has $u$ as a suffix, i.e., that $g(v_1u_1)=g(v_1)u$. Then $u=g|_{v_1}(u_1)$ and $g|_{v_1}\in\mathcal{N}$, hence $\mathcal{T}_{u_1}$ and $\mathcal{T}_u$ intersect. But $\mathcal{T}_{u_1}\subset\mathcal{T}_v$, hence $\mathcal{T}_v$ and $\mathcal{T}_u$ also intersect.

Suppose that $\mathcal{T}_v$ and $\mathcal{T}_u$ intersect. Then there exists a point of $\mathcal{J}_{G}$, which can be represented both by a sequence of the form $\ldots v_1u_1$ and by a sequence $\ldots v_0u\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$ for some $v_0\in\mathsf{X}^{|v_1|}$. It follows that these two sequences are asymptotically equivalent, hence by Proposition~\ref{pr:lims}, there exists $g\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $g(v_1u_1)=v_0u$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- defi-9: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a space with a log-scale $\ell$ (i.e., a function satisfying~\eqref{eq:logscale} for some $C$).  A metric $d$ on $\mathcal{X}$ is said to be a \emph{metric of exponent $\alpha$}, where $\alpha$ is a positive real number, if it satisfies
    \[d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\alpha\ell(\xi_1, \xi_2)}\]
    for all $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}$.
<!-- end defi-9 -->
<!-- defi-10: body_md -->
\label{def:lowerexponentforlog}
Let $\ell$ be a log-scale on a set $\mathcal{X}$. We say that $\alpha$ is a \emph{lower exponent} of $\ell$ if there exists $C>0$ such that for any $n$, any $\xi, \zeta\in\mathcal{X}$ and any sequence $\xi_0=\xi, \xi_1, \ldots, \xi_m=\zeta$ of points of $\mathcal{X}$ such that $\ell(\xi_i, \xi_{i+1})\ge n$ for all $i=1, \ldots, m-1$, we have
\[m\ge Ce^{\alpha(n-\ell(\xi, \zeta))}.\]
<!-- end defi-10 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
The supremum of values $\alpha$ for which $d_\alpha$ is a metric is equal to the supremum of the lower exponents of the log-scale $\ell$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
Let $d_\alpha$ and $\mu$ be a uniform metric of exponent $\alpha$ and the uniform measure on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$, respectively. Then there exists $C>1$ such that 
\[\mu(B_\xi(R))\asymp_C R^{\frac{\log \mathsf{D}}{\alpha}}\]
for every $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ and every $R<\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}\mathcal{J}_{G}$, where $\mathsf{D}=|\mathfrak{B}/G|$.

In particular, the Hausdorff dimension of $(\mathcal{J}_{G}, d_\alpha)$ is equal to $\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{\alpha}$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathsf{X}$ be a basis of $\mathfrak{B}$. We have $\mathsf{D}=|\mathsf{X}|$.
Let a point $\xi, \zeta\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ be represented by sequences $\ldots x_2x_1, \ldots y_2y_1\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$, respectively. The set $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} x_n\ldots x_2x_1$ belongs to the preimage of $T_\xi(n)$ in $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$ and \[\mu(T_\xi(n))\ge \mathsf{D}^{-n}.\] 

On the other hand, if $\zeta\in T_\xi(n)$, then $\zeta$ and $\xi$ belong to intersecting tiles of level $n$, hence there exist $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$ and $s\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $\xi\in\mathcal{T}_v$ and $\zeta\in\mathcal{T}_{s(v)}$. Therefore, there exists $s\in\mathcal{N}^3$ such that $y_n\ldots y_2y_1=s(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)$. It follows that the preimage of $\mathcal{T}_\xi(n)$ is contained in $\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal{N}^3}\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} s(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)$, hence \[\mu(T_\xi(n))\le|\mathcal{N}|^3\cdot\mathsf{D}^{-n}.\]

It is enough to prove the inequality in the proposition for all $R<R_0$ for some $R_0>0$. Let $C_0$ be such that
\[d_\alpha(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp_{C_0} e^{-\alpha\ell(\xi_1, \xi_2)}\] for all $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$.


Then, for every $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ and $R>0$, we have
\[T_\xi\left(-\log(C_0^{-1}R)/\alpha\right)\subseteq B_\xi(R)\subseteq T_\xi\left(-\log(C_0R)/\alpha\right).\]
Consequently, for all $R<C_0^{-1}$ and all $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$, we have
\[\mathsf{D}^{\log(C_0^{-1}R)/\alpha}\le\mu(B_\xi(R))\le |\mathcal{N}|^3\mathsf{D}^{\log(C_0R)/\alpha},\]
which is equivalent to
\[\mathsf{D}^{-\log C_0/\alpha}\cdot R^{\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{\alpha}}\le |\mathcal{N}|^3\mathsf{D}^{\log C_0/\alpha}\cdot R^{\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{\alpha}},\]
which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- defi-11: body_md -->
\label{def:AR}
Denote by $\mathcal{AR}=\mathcal{AR}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ the set of metrics $d$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ satisfying the following two conditions.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The metric $d$ is quasi-symmetric to uniform metrics on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$.
\item There exist $C>1$, $\alpha>0$, and a measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ such that
\[\mu(B_\xi(R))\asymp_C R^\alpha\]
for every $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ and $R\le\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}\mathcal{J}_{G}$.
\end{enumerate}

The \emph{(Ahlfors-regular) conformal dimension} $\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is the infimum of the Hausdorff dimensions of the metrics in the class $\mathcal{AR}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
<!-- end defi-11 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{pr:diamoftiles}
Choose a metric $d\in\mathcal{AR}(G, \mathfrak{B})$, and let $\mu$ be the associated Hausdorff measure of dimension $\alpha$. 

There exists a constant $C>1$ such that $\mu(\mathcal{T}_v)\asymp_C(\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}\mathcal{T}_v)^{\alpha}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$.

There exist $\lambda\in (0, 1)$ and $C>1$ such that $\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}\mathcal{T}_v\le C\lambda^{|v|}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since the tiles $\mathcal{T}\cdot g$ cover $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ and are closed, by the Baire category theorem, the interior of $\mathcal{T}$ is non-empty. Let $\xi$ be a point in the interior of $\mathcal{T}$. Then there exists $n_0$ such that $T_\xi(n_0)\subset\mathcal{T}$. Then for every $n\ge 1$ and $v\in\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n}$ we have $T_{\xi\otimes v}(n+n_0)\subset \mathcal{T}\otimes v$. Mapping these sets to $\mathcal{J}_{G}$, we get that every tile $\mathcal{T}_v$ of $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ contains a set of the form $T_\zeta(|v|+n_0)$ for some $\zeta\in\mathcal{T}_v$. Note that $\mathcal{T}_v\subset T_\zeta(|v|)$. It follows that there exist radii $r, R$ such that
\[B_\zeta(r)\subset\mathcal{T}_v\subset B_\zeta(R)\]
and $R/r\le C_1$ for some constant $C_1$. Condition (2) of Definition~\ref{def:AR} implies then that $\mu(\mathcal{T}_v)\asymp (\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}\mathcal{T}_v)^\alpha$, as $r<\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}\mathcal{T}_v<2R$.

It is shown in~\cite[Proposition~3.8]{mattebonnekzheng:liouvills} that $\sup_{\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}}\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}} T_n(\xi)\le C_2\lambda^n$ for some $C_2>0$ and $\lambda\in (0, 1)$, which implies the second statement of our proposition, since $\mathcal{T}_v\subset T_n(\xi)$ for every $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$ and $\xi\in\mathcal{T}_v$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- defi-12: body_md -->
\label{def:qcoc}
Let $G$ be a group acting on $\mathsf{X}^*$. A \emph{quasi-morphism} is a map $\nu\colon \mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ such that there exists $C>0$ such that
    \[\nu(v_1v_2)\doteq_C\nu(v_1)+\nu(v_2)\]
    for all $v_1, v_2\in\mathsf{X}^*$.

    We say that the quasi-morphism $\nu$ is \emph{positive} if 
    \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\nu(v)\to\infty.\]

    We say that it is \emph{$G$-quasi-invariant} if for every $g\in G$ there exists $C_g>0$ such that 
    \[\nu(g(v))\doteq_{C_g} \nu(v)\]
    for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$.
<!-- end defi-12 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
Let $\nu\colon \mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ be a positive quasi-morphism. There exists $\beta>0$ such that for every sufficiently large $R$ we have
\[|\{v\in\mathsf{X}^*\colon\nu(v)\le R\}|\asymp e^{\beta R}.\]
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Denote $V(R)=\{v\in\mathsf{X}^*\colon\nu(v)\le R\}$. It is finite, since $\nu(v)\asymp |v|$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$.

Let $m$ be such that $\nu(v)\ge C+1$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^m$, where $C$ is a constant satisfying the inequality in Definition~\ref{def:qcoc}. Let $M$ be the maximal value of $\nu(x)$ for $x\in\mathsf{X}$.

Let $R_1, R_2$ be arbitrary positive numbers. Consider a word $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ such that $\nu(v)\le R_1+R_2$. Let $v_1$ be the longest prefix of $v$ such that $\nu(v_1)\le R_1$. 
Let $v_2\in\mathsf{X}^*$ be such that $v=v_1v_2$. If $x$ is the first letter of $v_2$, then $R_1<\nu(v_1x)\le\nu(v_1)+\nu(x)+C\le\nu(v_1)+M+C$. Consequently, $\nu(v_1)>R_1-M-C$.


Then $\nu(v_1)+\nu(v_2)\le \nu(v_1v_2)+C\le R_1+R_2+C$, hence $\nu(v_2)\le R_1-\nu(v_1)+R_2+C<R_1-(R_1-M-\Delta)+R_2+C=
R_2+m+2C$. 

We have shown that every word $v$ such that $\nu(v)\le R_1+R_2$ can be split into two words $v=v_1v_2$ such that $\nu(v_1)\le R_1$ and $\nu(v_2)\le R_2+M+2C$. It follows that
\[|V(R_1+R_2)|\le |V(R_1)|\cdot |V(R_2+M+2C)|.\]
Equivalently,
\[|V(R_1+R_2-K)|\le|V(R_1)|\cdot |V(R_2)|\]
for $K=M+2C$ and all $R_1, R_2$ such that $R_1+R_2>K$.

Consider the function $\gamma(R)=|V(R+K)|$. 
Then, for all $R_1, R_2>0$, we have
\begin{multline*}\gamma(R_1+R_2)=|V(R_1+R_2+K)|=|V(R_1+K+R_2+K-K)|\le\\ 
|V(R_1+K)|\cdot|V(R_2+K)|=\gamma(R_1)\gamma(R_2).
\end{multline*}

It then follows from Fekete's Lemma that the limit $\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{\log\gamma(R)}{R}$ exists and is equal to $\inf_{R>0}\frac{\log |V(R+K)|}{R}$. Let us denote the limit by $\beta$. We have 
\[|V(R+K)|\ge e^{\beta R}\] for all $R>0$,
hence 
\[C_1e^{\beta R}\le |V(R)|\]
for $C_1=e^{-\beta K}$ and all $R>K$.

On the other hand, for any pair $R_1, R_2>0$,  the map $V(R_1)\times V(R_2)\colon (v_1, v_2)\mapsto v_1v_2$ takes values in $V(R_1+R_2+C)$ and is injective. Consequently,
\[|V(R_1+R_2+C)|\ge |V(R_1)|\cdot |V(R_2)|\]
for all $R_1, R_2>0$.
The function $\gamma(R)=|V(R-C)|$ satisfies then
\begin{multline*}
    \gamma(R_1+R_2)=|V(R_1+R_2-C)|=|V(R_1-C+R_2-C+C)|\ge\\
    |V(R_1-C)|\cdot|V(R_2-C)|=\gamma(R_1)\gamma(R_2).
\end{multline*}
Consequently, the limit $\beta=\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{\log\gamma(R)}R$ is equal to the supremum of $\frac{\log\gamma(R)}R$, consequently,
\[\frac{\log|V(R-C)|}R\le\beta\]
for all $R>C$, i.e., 
\[|V(R-C)|\le e^{\beta R},\]
which gives us the estimate
\[|V(R)|\le C_2e^{\beta R}\]
for $C_2=e^{\beta C}$ and all $R>0$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{pr:entropycriterion}
    Let $\nu$ be a positive quasi-morphism, and let $\beta$ be the $\nu$-entropy. Suppose that $\beta_0>0$ is such that there exists $\lambda\in (0, 1)$ such that for every $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ we have
    \[\sum_{x\in\mathsf{X}}e^{-\beta_0\nu(xv)}\le\lambda e^{-\beta_0\nu(v)}.\]
    Then $\beta\le\beta_0$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The inequality in the proposition implies that for every $n$ and $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ we have
\[\sum_{u\in\mathsf{X}^n}e^{-\beta_0\nu(uv)}\le \lambda^n e^{-\beta_0\nu(v)}.\]

It follows that the series $\Lambda=\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*}e^{-\beta_0\nu(v)}$ is convergent.

Consider the set $V(R)=\{v\in\mathsf{X}^*\colon\nu(v)\le R\}$. For 
every $v\in V(R)$, we have $e^{-\beta_0\nu(v)}\ge e^{-\beta_0 R}$. Consequently, $\Lambda\ge |V(R)|\cdot e^{-\beta_0 R}$, hence $|V(R)|\le\Lambda e^{\beta_0 R}$ for all $R$, which implies that $\beta\le\beta_0$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
Let $\nu$ be a positive quasi-morphism, and let $\beta$ be the $\nu$-entropy.

    There exist measures $\mu_+$ and $\mu_-$ on $\mathsf{X}^\omega$ and $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$, respectively, such
    \[\mu_+(v\mathsf{X}^\omega)\asymp e^{-\beta\nu(v)}\asymp\mu_-(\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} v)\]
    for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$.

    If $\nu$ is $G$-quasi-invariant for an action of $G$ by automorphisms of the rooted tree $\mathsf{X}^*$, then the measure $\mu_+$ is quasi-invariant under the action of $G$ on $\mathsf{X}^\omega$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let us prove the first statement of the theorem for $\mathsf{X}^\omega$, the proof for $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$ is the same.

Consider $\mathsf{X}^\omega\cup\mathsf{X}^*$ as the natural compactification of $\mathsf{X}^*$ by $\mathsf{X}^\omega$.
    For every $s>\beta$, and a continuous function $f\colon \mathsf{X}^\omega\cup\mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$, consider the series
\[\mathcal{P}_s(f)=\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*}f(v)e^{-s\nu(v)}.\]
It is a positive linear functional on $C(\mathsf{X}^\omega\cup\mathsf{X}^*)$.

Let $C$ be such that \[C^{-1}e^{\beta R}\le |\{v\in\mathsf{X}^*\colon\nu(v)\le R\}|\le C e^{\beta R}\]
for all $R>0$.

Let $S(n)=\{v\in\mathsf{X}^*\colon n-1< \nu(v)\le n\}$.
Then  we have
\begin{multline*}\mathcal{P}_s(f)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{v\in S(n)}f(v)e^{-s\nu(v)}\le C\|f\|_\infty\sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{-s(n-1)}e^{\beta n}=\\ 
C\|f\|_\infty\sum_{n=0}^\infty e^{-sn}e^{\beta(n+1)}=
Ce^\beta\|f\|_\infty\sum_{n=0}^\infty e^{(\beta-s)n}=\frac{C_1\|f\|_\infty}{1-e^{\beta-s}}.
\end{multline*}

Define the measure $\mu_s$ on $\mathsf{X}^*\cup\mathsf{X}^\omega$ by
\[\int f\;d\mu_s=(1-e^{\beta-s})\mathcal{P}_s(f)\]
for all continuous functions $f\colon \mathsf{X}^*\cup\mathsf{X}^\omega\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$. By the above, we have $\int f\;d\mu_s\le C_1\|f\|_\infty$ for all $f\in C(\mathsf{X}^*\cup\mathsf{X}^\omega)$ and all $s>\beta$.

It follows from the Uniform Boundedness Principle that the set $\{\mu_s\colon s>\beta\}$ is bounded in the dual of $C(\mathsf{X}^*\cup\mathsf{X}^\omega)$. Hence, by the Banach-Alaoglu Theorem, there exists a weakly convergent sequence $\mu_{s_k}$ for $s_k\to\beta+$. Let $\mu$ be its limit. 

For every $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$, the sequence $(1-e^{\beta-s_k})e^{-s_k\nu(v)}$ converges to 0, hence $\mu$ is supported on $\mathsf{X}^\omega$.

Let $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$, and let $\xi_v$ be the indicator of $v\mathsf{X}^*\cup v\mathsf{X}^\omega$ (which is a continuous function). Then
\[\mu(v\mathsf{X}^\omega)=\lim_{k\to\infty}(1-e^{\beta-s_k})\sum_{w\in\mathsf{X}^*}e^{-s_k\nu(vw)}.\]
We have \[e^{-s_k(\nu(w)+\nu(v)+C)}\le e^{-s_k\nu(vw)}\le e^{-s_k(\nu(w)+\nu(v)-C)}.\]
Multiplying the inequalities by $(1-e^{\beta-s})$ and adding them over all $w\in\mathsf{X}^*$, we get
\[e^{-C}e^{-s_k\nu(v)}\mu_{s_k}(\mathsf{X}^*\cup\mathsf{X}^\omega)\le\mu_{s_k}(v\mathsf{X}^*\cup v\mathsf{X}^\omega)\le e^C e^{-s_k\nu(v)}\mu_{s_k}(\mathsf{X}^*\cup\mathsf{X}^\omega).\] Passing to the limit, we get
\[K_1 e^{-\beta\nu(v)}\le\mu(v\mathsf{X}^\omega)\le K_2 e^{-\beta\nu(v)}\]
for $K_1=e^{-\Delta}\mu(\mathsf{X}^\omega)$ and $K_2=e^\Delta\mu(\mathsf{X}^\omega)$.

Note that, as a consequence of the estimates, we get that for any $v_1, v_2\in\mathsf{X}^*$, the measure $\mu$ is quasi-invariant under the transformation $w\mapsto vw$ with the Radon-Nikodym derivative belonging to the interval $(C_1^{-1}e^{-\beta\nu(v)}, C_1e^{-\beta\nu(v)})$ for a  constant $C_1$, not depending on $v$.

It follows that in order to show that $\mu$ is quasi-invariant under the action of $G$, it is enough to show that it is quasi-invariant under the action of the elements of the nucleus. But this follows from an estimate $\nu(s(v))\doteq \nu(v)$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ and $s\in\mathcal{N}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- defi-13: body_md -->
Let $\nu\colon\mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ be a quasi-invariant quasi-morphism for a self-similar contracting group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$. Then the \emph{$\nu$-dimension} $\dim_\nu(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is the infimum of the Hausdorff dimensions of the visual metrics $d_{\nu, \alpha}$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$.
<!-- end defi-13 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{pr:quasimorphismsquasisymmetric}
Any two visual metrics associated with positive $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphisms are quasi-symmetric to each other.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
It is enough to show that the visual metric associated with a positive $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism $\nu$ is quasi-symmetric to a uniform metric.

Let $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$, and let $\ldots x_2x_1$ be a sequence representing it. Denote 
\[\beta(n)=\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1).\]

There exist constants $\Delta>0$ and $C_1>1$ such that
\[\beta(n_1)-\beta(n_2)\doteq_{\Delta}\nu(x_{n_1}x_{n_1-1}\ldots x_{n_2+1})\]
and
\[\nu(x_{n_1}\ldots x_{n_2+1})\asymp_{C_1} n_1-n_2\]
for all $n_1>n_2$.

It follows that 
\[
\beta(n_1)-\beta(n_2)\ge\left\{\begin{array}{rr}
C^{-1}(n_1-n_2)-\Delta & \text{if $n_1\ge n_2$}\\
C(n_1-n_2)-\Delta & \text{if $n_1<n_2$.}
\end{array}\right.
\]
Denote $\gamma(n)=C^{-\mathop{\mathrm{sign}}(n)}n$, so that we have
\[\beta(n_1)-\beta(n_2)\ge\gamma(n_1-n_2)-\Delta\]
for all $n_1, n_2$. Note that $\gamma$ is a strictly increasing homeomorphism $\gamma\colon \mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$.



By the definition of the functions $\ell_\nu$ and $\ell$ (i.e., the function $\ell_{|\cdot|}$), there exists $\Delta_1>0$ such that
\[\ell_\nu(\xi, \eta)\doteq_{\Delta_1}\beta(\ell(\xi, \eta))\]
for all $\eta\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$.

Let $\alpha$ and $\alpha_0$ be such that the visual metric $|\cdot|_{\nu, \alpha}$ and the uniform metric $|\cdot|_{\alpha_0}$ are defined.

Then there exist  constants $C_i>1$ such that
\begin{multline*}\frac{d_{\nu, \alpha}(\xi, \eta)}{d_{\nu, \alpha}(\xi, \zeta)}\le C_1e^{-\alpha(\ell_\nu(\xi, \eta)-\ell_\nu(\xi, \zeta))}\le C_1e^{2\alpha\Delta_1}e^{-\alpha(\beta(\ell(\xi, \eta))-\beta(\ell(\xi, \zeta)))}\le \\
C_2e^{-\alpha \gamma(\ell(\xi, \eta)-\ell(\xi, \zeta))}.
\end{multline*}

There also exist a constants $C_3>1$ and $C_4>0$ such that
\[\frac{d_{\alpha_0}(\xi, \eta)}{d_{\alpha_0}(\xi, \zeta)}\ge C_3^{-1}e^{-\alpha_0(\ell(\xi, \eta)-\ell(\xi, \zeta))},\]
hence
\[\ell(\xi, \eta)-\ell(\xi, \zeta)\ge -\alpha_0^{-1}\log\left(\frac{d_{\alpha_0}(\xi, \eta)}{d_{\alpha_0}(\xi, \zeta)}\right)-C_4\]



Consequently, 
\[\frac{d_{\nu, \alpha}(\xi, \eta)}{d_{\nu, \alpha}(\xi, \zeta)}\le\eta\left(\frac{d_{\alpha_0}(\xi, \eta)}{d_{\alpha_0}(\xi, \zeta)}\right)\]
for
\[\eta(t)=C_2\exp\left(-\alpha\gamma\left(-\alpha_0^{-1}\log t-C_4\right)\right),\]
which shows that $d_{\nu, \alpha}$ and $d_{\alpha_0}$ are quasi-symmetric.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
Note that metrics on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ associated with two quasi-morphisms $\nu_1\colon(\mathsf{X}^n)^*\longrightarrow (0, \infty)$ and $\nu_2\colon(\mathsf{X}^m)^*\longrightarrow(0, \infty)$ are quasi-symmetric to each other.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Restrict the quasi-morphisms to $(\mathsf{X}^{nm})^*$ and then use Proposition~\ref{pr:quasimorphismsquasisymmetric} for the self-similar group $(G, \mathfrak{B}^{\otimes nm})$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
Let $\nu\colon \mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ be a positive $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism. Let $\beta$ be the $\nu$-entropy.

Consider a visual metric $d_{\nu, \alpha}$, and let $\mu$ be the push forward to $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ of the measure on $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$ associated with $\nu$. Let $B_\xi(R)$ denote the ball of radius $R$ with center in $\xi$ defined using the metric $d_{\nu, \alpha}$. Then there exists a constant $C>1$ such that
\[\mu(B_\xi(R))\asymp_C R^{\beta/\alpha}\]
for all $R<\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}\mathcal{J}_{G}$ and $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $\ldots x_2x_1\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$ be a sequence representing $\xi$. Then, for some constants $C_1>1$, the neighborhood $T_\xi(n)$ contains the ball $B_\xi(C_1^{-1}e^{-\alpha\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)})$ and is contained in the ball $B_\xi(C_1e^{-\alpha\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)})$. 

The preimage of the set $T_\xi(n)$ in $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$ contains $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} x_n\ldots x_2x_1$ and is contained in $\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}^3}\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} g(x_n\ldots x_1)$. Since $\nu$ is $G$-quasi-invariant, it follows that there exists a constant  $C_2>1$ such that
\[C_2^{-1}e^{-\beta\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)}\le\mu(T_\xi(n))\le C_2e^{-\beta\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)}.\]

Consequently, for $R_n=e^{-\alpha\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)}$, we have
\[\mu(B_\xi(C_1^{-1}R_n))\le\mu(T_\xi(n))\le C_2 R_n^{\beta/\alpha}\]
and
\[\mu(B_\xi(C_1R_n))\ge\mu(T_\xi(n))\ge C_2^{-1}R_n^{\beta/\alpha}.\]

Let $R\in (0, R_1)$. Let $n_1$ be the maximum of the set of natural numbers $n$ such that $C_1^{-1}R_n\ge R$, which exists, since $R_n\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$. Let $n_0$ be the minimum of the set of natural numbers $n$ such that $C_1R_n\le R$. Since the ratio $R_n/R_{n+1}$ is bounded from below and from above by positive constants, the ratios $R_{n_0}/R$ and $R_{n_1}/R$ are also bounded from below and from above by positive constants.

We have 
\[\mu(B_\xi(R))\le\mu(B_\xi(R_{n_1}))\le C_2R_{n_1}^{\beta/\alpha}\le C_3R^{\beta/\alpha}\]
and
\[\mu(B_\xi(R))\ge\mu(C_1R_{n_0})\ge C_2^{-1}R_{n_0}^{\beta/\alpha}\ge C_3^{-1}R^{\beta/\alpha}\]
for some constant $C_3>1$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{pr:Sv1Sv2}
Suppose that $A_{n_1, v_1}$ and $A_{n_2, v_2}$ are isomorphic. Then the map \[S_{v_1, v_2}\colon \bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}^2}\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} g(v_1)\longrightarrow\bigcup_{g\in\mathcal{N}^2}\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} g(v_2)\colon wg(v_1)\mapsto wg(v_2)\]
induces a well defined homeomorphism $\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_1}\longrightarrow\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_2}$.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since $A_{n_1, v_1}$ and $A_{n_2, v_2}$ are isomorphic, $g_1(v_1)=g_2(v_1)$ for $g_1, g_2\in\mathcal{N}^2$ is equivalent to $g_1(v_2)=g_2(v_2)$, hence the map $wg(v_1)\mapsto wg(v_2)$ is well defined.

Since the cylindrical sets $\mathsf{X}^{-\omega} v$ are compact, it is enough to show that the maps $S_{v_1, v_2}$ preserve the equivalence relation. A sequence $\ldots x_2x_1g_1(v_1)$ is equivalent to $\ldots y_2y_1g_2(v_1)$ if and only if there exists a sequence $s_n\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $s_n\cdot x_n=y_n\cdot s_{n-1}$ and $s_0g_1(v_1)=g_2(v_1)$. The latter condition is equivalent to $s_0g_1(v_2)=g_2(v_2)$. Therefore, the same sequence $s_n$ will show that $S_{v_1, v_2}(\ldots x_2x_1g_1(v_1))=S_{v_1, v_2}(\ldots y_2y_1g_2(v_1))$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{pr:localssimilarities}
Let $d_{\nu, \alpha}$ be a visual metric of exponent $\alpha$ associated with a quasi-morphism $\nu$. There exists $C>1$ such that for every pair $v_1, v_2$ such that the homeomorphism $S_{v_1, v_2}\colon \widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_1}\longrightarrow\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_2}$ is defined,  we have
\[\frac{d_{\nu, \alpha}(S_{v_1, v_2}(\xi_1), S_{v_1, v_2}(\xi_2))}{d_{\nu, \alpha}(\xi_1, \xi_2)}\asymp_C e^{-\alpha(\nu(v_2)-\nu(v_1))}\]
for every pair $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_1}$ of different points.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $k_0\ge 1$ be such that $\mathcal{N}^2|_{\mathsf{X}^{k_0}}=\mathcal{N}$.

Let $\xi_1, \xi_2\in \widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_1}$. Then $\xi_i$ can be represented by sequences $\ldots x_2x_1g_1(v_1)$ and $\ldots y_2y_1g_2(v_1)$ for some $g_1, g_2\in\mathcal{N}$.  Then $\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)\ge \nu(v_1)-C$ for some uniform constant $C$. Since $\nu$ is a quasi-morphism, we have
\[\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)\doteq \nu(x_m\ldots x_2x_1)+\nu(v_1),\] where $m$ is the largest index such that $g(x_m\ldots x_2x_1)=y_m\ldots y_2y_1$ for some $g\in\mathcal{N}^3$. Similarly, 
\[\ell_\nu(S_{v_1, v_2}(\xi_1), S_{v_1, v_2}(\xi_2))\doteq \nu(x_m\ldots x_2x_1)+\nu(v_2).\] It follows that \[\ell_\nu(S_{v_1, v_2}(\xi_1), S_{v_1, v_2}(\xi_2))\doteq \ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)+\nu(v_2)-\nu(v_1),\] which implies the estimate of the proposition.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{pr:uniformlocalsim}
A metric $d$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ is a visual metric associated with a $G$-quasi-invariant positive quasi-morphism $\nu\colon\mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow[0, \infty)$ if and only if there exist $L>1$ and $\delta>0$ such that for every $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ and every $n\ge 1$ there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $\xi$ such that $f^n\colon U\longrightarrow B_{f^n(\xi)}(\delta)/D$ is an $L$-bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism for some $D>0$ (depending on $\xi$ and $n$).
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Let us first prove that a visual metric $d_{\nu, \alpha}$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition.

By the regularity condition, there exists $k_0$ such that for every $g\in\mathcal{N}^3$ and every $v\in\mathsf{X}^{k_0}$ we have either $g(v)\ne v$ or $g(v)=v$ and $g|_v=1$.

Then the isomorphism class of $A_{n, u}$ for $u\in\mathsf{X}^n$, $n\ge k_0$, depends only on the prefix of length $k$ of the word $u$.
Consequently, the restriction of $f^n$ to $\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0v}$ for $v_0\in\mathsf{X}^{k_0}, v\in\mathsf{X}^n$ is the homeomorphism $S_{v_0v, v_0}\colon \widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0v}\longrightarrow\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0}$, satisfying Proposition~\ref{pr:localssimilarities}. Hence there exists a constant $L>1$, not depending on $v_0$ and $v$, such that $f^n$ restricted to $\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0v}$ is an $L$-bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism to $\frac 1D\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0}$ for some $D$.

For every $\xi\in\mathcal{T}_{v_0}$ we have $T_\xi(k_0)\subset\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0}$. There exists $\delta>0$ such that $B_\xi(\delta)\subset T_\xi(k_0)$ for all $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$. Then, for every $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ and $n$, we can take $U$ equal to the preimage of $B_{f^n(\xi)}(\delta)$ under the homeomorphism $S_{v_0v, v_0}\colon \widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0v}\longrightarrow\widetilde\mathcal{T}_{v_0}$, where $v_0\in\mathsf{X}^{k_0}$ and $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$ are such that $\xi\in\mathcal{T}_{v_0v}$.

Conversely, suppose that $d$ satisfies the conditions of the proposition. There exists $k_1\ge k_0$ such that $\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}_v)<\delta$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^{k_1}$.


Let $\xi$ be a point of $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ represented by a sequence $\ldots x_2x_1\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$.
We have \[f^{n-k_1}(\mathcal{T}_{x_n\ldots x_1})\subset\mathcal{T}_{x_n\ldots x_{n-k_1+1}}\subset B_{f^{n-k_1}(\xi)}(\delta).\]
Consequently, there exists $D=D_{x_n\ldots x_2x_1}$ such that we have 
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Dv}
d(f^{n-k_1}(\xi_1), f^{n-k_1}(\xi_2))\asymp_L D_{x_n\ldots x_2x_1}d(\xi_1, \xi_2)
\end{equation}
for all pairs of different points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{x_n\ldots x_2x_1}$.


Consider a word $x_{n+k_1}\ldots x_2x_1$, and two points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{x_{n+k_1}\ldots x_2x_1}$. Denote $\zeta_i=f^{n-k_1}(\xi_i)$. 
Since $\xi_i\in\mathcal{T}_{x_n\ldots x_2x_1}$, the estimate~\eqref{eq:Dv} is written as
\[d(\zeta_1, \zeta_2)\asymp_L D_{x_n\ldots x_2x_1}d(\xi_1, \xi_2).\]
We have $\zeta_i\in\mathcal{T}_{x_{n+k_1}\ldots x_{n-k_1+1}}$, so, using~\eqref{eq:Dv} with $\xi_i$ replaced by $\zeta_i$ and $n$ by $2k_1$, we get
\[d(f^n(\xi_1), f^n(\xi_2))=d(f^{k_1}(\zeta_1), f^{k_1}(\zeta_2))\asymp_L
D_{x_{n+k_1}\ldots x_{n-k_1+1}}d(\zeta_1, \zeta_2)\asymp_{L_1} d(\zeta_1, \zeta_2),\]
where $L_1=\max_{v\in\mathsf{X}^{2k_1}}D_v$.
It follows that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Dv2}
d(f^n(\xi_1), f^n(\xi_2))\asymp_{L^2L_1}D_{x_n\ldots x_2x_1}d(\xi_1, \xi_2)
\end{equation}
for all $n\ge k_1$ and $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{x_{n+k_1}\ldots x_2x_1}$. 

For every $v\in\mathsf{X}^{n+k_1}$, the set $f^n(\mathcal{T}_v)$ is a tile of the level $k_1$, so it has diameter less than $\delta$. Consequently, by the condition of the proposition, the restriction of $f^n$ to $\mathcal{T}_v$ is bi-Lipschitz.
Since the number of words $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ of a given length is finite, we can choose $L$ large enough and define $D_v=1$ for all $|v|<k_1$, so that the estimate~\eqref{eq:Dv} holds for all words $x_n\ldots x_2x_1$ and all $\xi_1, \xi_2$ contained in one tile of the level $n+k_1$.



Consider now a word $x_{n+m+k_1}\ldots x_2x_1$ for some $n, m\ge 0$. Choose two points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{x_{n+m+k_1}\ldots x_2x_1}$. Then, by the proven above, we have
\[d(f^{n+m}(\xi_1), f^{n+m}(\xi_2))\asymp_{L^2L_1} D_{x_{n+m}\ldots x_2x_1}d(\xi_1, \xi_2).\]

We have $f^m(\xi_i)\in \mathcal{T}_{x_{n+m+k_1}\ldots x_{m+2}x_{m+1}}$, so
\[d(f^{n+m}(\xi_1), f^{n+m}(\xi_2))\asymp_{L^2L_1} D_{x_{n+m}\ldots x_{m+2}x_{m+1}}d(f^m(\xi_1), f^m(\xi_2)).\]
We also have $\xi_i\in\mathcal{T}_{x_{m+k_1}\ldots x_2x_1}$, so
\[d(f^m(\xi_1), f^m(\xi_2))\asymp_{L^2L_1} D_{x_m\ldots x_2x_1}d(\xi_1, \xi_2).\]

We proved that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Dmorphism}
D_{x_{n+m}\ldots x_1}\asymp_{L^4L_1} D_{x_{n+m}\ldots x_{n+1}}D_{x_n\ldots x_2x_1}
\end{equation}
for all words $x_{n+m}\ldots x_2x_1$.

Since $f$ is locally expanding, $\max_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}D_v$ converges to $0$ as $v\to\infty$. Consequently, the estimate~\eqref{eq:Dmorphism} implies that $\nu(v)=-\log D_v$ extends to a positive quasi-morphism $\nu\colon \mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow[0, \infty)$.

Let us show that $\nu$ is $G$-quasi-invariant. Let $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ and $g\in\mathcal{N}$. Then $\mathcal{T}_v\cap\mathcal{T}_{g(v)}\ne\emptyset$. Let $\xi\in\mathcal{T}_v\cap \mathcal{T}_{g(v)}$, and let $\ldots x_2x_1, \ldots y_2y_1$ be sequences representing $\xi$ such that $x_n\ldots x_2x_1=v$ and $y_n\ldots y_2y_1=g(v)$. We assume that $n\ge k_1$. Then $f^{n-k_1}(\mathcal{T}_v\cup\mathcal{T}_{g(v)})$ is contained in $B_{f^n(\xi)}(\delta)$, so 
\[d(f^{n-k_1}(\xi_1), f^{n-k_1}(\xi_2))\asymp_L Dd(\xi_1, \xi_2)\]
for all $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_v\cup\mathcal{T}_{g(v)}$. It follows that $D\asymp_{L^2} D_v$ and $D\asymp_{L^2} D_{g(v)}$. Consequently, $D_v\asymp_{L^4} D_{g(v)}$, hence $\nu$ is $G$-quasi-invariant.

Let us show that $d$ is bi-Lipschitz equivalent to a visual metric $d_{\nu, 1}$ of exponent $\alpha=1$ associated with $\nu$. Let $\ldots x_2x_1, \ldots y_2y_1\in\mathsf{X}^{-\omega}$ represent the points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$, and let $n$ be the largest index such that $g(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)=y_n\ldots y_2y_1$ for some $g\in\mathcal{N}$. Then $d_{\nu, 1}(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)}$. 

On the other hand, by the same arguments as in the proof of $G$-quasi-invariance of $\nu$, we have \[d(f^{n-k_1}(\xi_1), f^{n-k_1}(\xi_2))\asymp e^{\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)}d(\xi_1, \xi_2).\]

By Proposition~\ref{pr:localssimilarities}, we have
\[d_{\nu, 1}(f^{n-k_1}(\xi_1)-f^{n-k_1}(\xi_2))\asymp e^{\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)}d_{\nu, 1}(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp 1.\]
Since $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ is compact, this implies that there exists a uniform constants $\epsilon>0$ independent of $\xi_1, \xi_2$ such that 
\[\epsilon^{-1}>d(f^{n-k_1}(\xi_1), f^{n-k_1}(\xi_2))>\epsilon.\]
Consequently, $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\nu(x_n\ldots x_2x_1)}\asymp d_{\nu, 1}(\xi_1, \xi_2)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
Let $f$ be a hyperbolic complex rational function. It follows from Koebe distortion theorem that the spherical metric on the Riemann sphere restricted to the Julia set of $f$ satisfies the condition of Proposition~\ref{pr:uniformlocalsim}. (See also a direct proof of it in~\cite[Proposition~3.7]{nek:psmeasure}.) Consequently, it is bi-Lipschitz to a visual metric associated with a quasi-morphism.
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- defi-14: body_md -->
\label{def:liftofmetric}
    The \emph{lift} of $d$ to $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ is defined for $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$ as the infimum $\tilde d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ of the expression
\[\sum_{i=1}^m\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i)),\]
over all sequences $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\in\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n}$ and all $n$ such that $\xi_1\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_1$, $\xi_2\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_m$ and $\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i\cap\mathcal{T}\otimes v_{i+1}\ne\emptyset$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, m-1$. The function $\tilde d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ is defined to be infinite if such a sequence does not exist.
<!-- end defi-14 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
The function $\tilde d$ is a $G$-invariant metric (with infinite distances allowed) compatible with the topology on $\mathcal{X}_{G}$.

The map $P\colon(\mathcal{X}_{G}, \tilde d)\longrightarrow(\mathcal{J}_{G}, d)$ is distance non-increasing. For every $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ the diameter of $\mathcal{T}\otimes v$ in $(\mathcal{X}_{G}, \tilde d)$ is equal to the diameter of $\mathcal{T}_v=P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)$ in $(\mathcal{J}_{G}, d)$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
It is easy to check that 
the defined function $\tilde d$ satisfies the triangle inequality, is symmetric, and $G$-invariant. 

Let $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$. 
Let $(v_i)$ be a sequence satisfying the conditions of Definition~\ref{def:liftofmetric}. Choose a point $\zeta_i\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i\cap\mathcal{T}\otimes v_{i+1}$ for every $i=1, 2, \ldots, m-1$, and set $\zeta_0=\xi_1$ and $\zeta_m=\xi_2$. Then we have \[d(P(\xi_1), P(\xi_2))\le
\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}d(P(\zeta_i), P(\zeta_{i+1}))\le 
\sum_{i=1}^m\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i)),\]
since $\zeta_{i-1}, \zeta_i\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i$. Consequently, $d(P(\xi_1), P(\xi_2))\le\tilde d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$.

If $\xi_1\ne\xi_2$, then there exists $n$ such that the neighborhoods $T_n(\xi_i)$ are disjoint. Then $P(T_n(\xi_i))$ is a neighborhood of $P(\xi_i)$, since $P$ is open (see, for example, the proof of~\cite[Proposition~2.19]{nek:dimension}). Let $\epsilon>0$ be the distance from $P(\xi_1)$ to the complement of $P(T_n(\xi_1))$. Then for any chain in the definition of $\tilde d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ the corresponding sum of diameters is greater than the minimal diameter of $\mathcal{T}_v$ for $|v|<n$, or is greater than $\epsilon$. It follows that $\tilde d(\xi_1, \xi_2)>0$ for any $\xi_1\ne \xi_2$.



For any two points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in \mathcal{T}\otimes v$ we have $\tilde d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\le\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v))$, hence $\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}_{\tilde d}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)\le\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}_d(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v))$. On the other hand, since $P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)$ is compact, there exist $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v$ such that $d(P(\xi_1), P(\xi_2))=\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v))$. Then $\tilde d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\ge d(P(\xi_1), P(\xi_2))=\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v))$.
Consequently, 
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:diamforlift}
    \mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)=\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v))
\end{equation}
for all $v\in\mathfrak{B}^*$.
 
The equality $\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)=\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(P(\mathcal{T}\otimes v))$ implies that this metric is compatible with the topology, since the sets $T_n(\xi)$ form a basis of neighborhoods of a point $\xi$ both in $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ and in $\mathcal{J}_{G}$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
Consider the adding machine from Example~\ref{ex:angledoubling}. Its $n$th level dual Moore diagram is a cycle of $2^n$ edges, with all labels trivial except for the arrow from $11\ldots 1$ to $00\ldots 0$ labeled by $a$. Then every essential path makes a full loop and contains all arrows of the diagram.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- example-10: body_md -->
The $n$th level dual Moore diagram of the Grigorchuk group~\cite{grig85_en} is a chain from $11\ldots 10$ to $11\ldots 11$ consisting of multiple edges and loops such that all their labels are trivial except for the labels $b, c, d$ of three loops at $11\ldots 11$ and two loops labeled by $a$ at $11\ldots 10$. Since $\{1, b, c, d\}$ and $\{1, a\}$ are groups contained in the nucleus, every essential path must pass through $11\ldots 10$ and $11\ldots 11$.
<!-- end example-10 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\overline{\mathcal{A}}$ be the sets of admissible functions on $\mathsf{X}^n$ and $S\times\mathsf{X}^n$, respectively. Then for every $p\in [1, \infty]$ we have $M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)\asymp_{C_p} M_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n)$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $\phi\colon\mathsf{X}^n\longrightarrow[0, \infty)$ be an admissible function.
If $e$ is an edge starting in $v_1$ and ending in $v_2$, then define $\phi_1(e)=\phi(v_1)+\phi(v_2)$. Then $\phi_1$ is an admissible function on the set of edges and we have \[\phi_1^p(e)=(\phi(v_1)+\phi(v_2))^p\le \max(1, 2^{p-1})(\phi(v_1)^p+\phi(v_2)^p),\]
if $p$ is finite.

 It follows that \[\sum\phi_1^p(e)\le \max(1, 2^{p-1})|S|\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\phi(v)^p.\] Consequently, \[M_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n)\le\max(1, 2^{p-1})|S| \cdot M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n).\]
  
 We also obviously have $\max\phi_1(e)\le 2\max\phi(v)$, so $M_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}, \infty}(n)\le 2M_{\mathcal{A}, \infty}(n)$.

On the other hand, suppose that $\phi$ is an admissible function on the set of edges. Define $\phi_0(v)$ as the sum $\sum_{s\in S}\phi(s, v)$ of values of $\phi$ in all edges adjacent to $v$. Then $\phi_0$ is admissible. We have $\phi_0(v)^p\le |S|^{p-1}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{N}} \phi(s, v)^p$, hence \[\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\phi_0(v)^p\le 2|S|^{p-1}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{N}, v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\phi(s, v)^p.\]

 Consequently, $M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)\le 2|S|^{p-1} M_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n)$.
Similarly, $M_{\mathcal{A}, \infty}(n)\le 2|S| M_{\overline{\mathcal{A}}, \infty}(n)$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{pr:moduluschanginggenset}
Let $N$ be a finite subset of $G$ containing the nucleus $\mathcal{N}$, and let $S$ be a finite symmetric generating set, also containing the nucleus.
Let $\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}$ be the set of $\mathcal{N}$-admissible functions on the set of edges of the graph $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}}$. Let $\mathcal{A}_S$ be the set of $N$-admissible functions on the set of edges of $\Gamma_{n, S}$.

Then $M_{\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}, p}(n)\asymp_C M_{\mathcal{A}_S, p}(n)$, where $C$ does not depend on $n$.
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
There exists $n_1$ such that for every $s\in S$ and every $v\in\mathsf{X}^{n_1}$ we have $g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$.
Let $n>n_1$, and consider the map $P\colon \Gamma_{n, S}\longrightarrow\Gamma_{n-n_1, \mathcal{N}}$ mapping an edge $(s, x_1x_2\ldots x_n)$ of $\Gamma_{n, S}$ to the edge $g|_{x_1x_2\ldots x_{n_1}}, x_{n_1+1}x_{n_1+2}\ldots x_n)$ of $\Gamma_{n-n_1, \mathcal{N}}$. In other words, we remove the prefix of length $n_1$ and replace $s$ by the corresponding section. The map $P$ is  $|\mathsf{X}^{n_1}|$-to-one.

Let $\phi$ be an admissible (i.e., $\mathcal{N}$-admissible) function on the set of edges of $\Gamma_{n-n_1, \mathcal{N}}$. Define the function $\tilde\phi$ on $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{S}}$ by $\tilde\phi(e)=\phi(P(e))$.

For every $N$-essential edge path $\gamma$ in $\Gamma_{n, S}$, the corresponding sections of $\gamma$ and $P(\gamma)$ coincide. Since the former does not belong to $N$, the latter does not belong to $\mathcal{N}\subset N$. Consequently, $P(\gamma)$ is also essential. Consequently, the sum of values of $\phi$ along the edges of $P(\gamma)$ is not less than 1. But it is equal to the sum of values of $\tilde\phi$ along the edges of $\gamma$. Consequently, $\tilde\phi$ is admissible. We have $\sum\left(\tilde\phi(e)\right)^p\le |\mathsf{X}|^{n_1}\sum\phi(e)^p$. Consequently, \[M_{\mathcal{A}_S, p}(n)\le |\mathsf{X}|^{n_1}\cdot M_{\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}, p}(n)\] for all $n$.

Suppose now that $\phi$ is an $N$-admissible function on $\Gamma_{n, S}$. Let $n_2$ be such that for every $h\in N$ and $v\in\mathsf{X}^{n_2}$ we have $h|_v\in\mathcal{N}$.
Let $\gamma$ be a path in $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}}$ connecting a vertex $x_1x_2\ldots x_n$ to $y_1y_2\ldots y_n$, and let $g\in G$ be the corresponding product such that $g(x_1x_2\ldots x_n)=y_1y_2\ldots y_n$. There exists $r$ such that every element of $\mathcal{N}$ is a product of elements of $S$.

Let $\gamma'$ be the path in $\Gamma_{n, S}$ obtained by replacing each edge $(s_i, v_i)$ by the path in $\Gamma_{n, S}$ corresponding to the decomposition of $s_i$ as a product of elements of $S$. The path $\gamma'$ has the same endpoints as $\gamma$, and the same product $g$.

Suppose that $\gamma$ is essential, i.e., $g|_{x_1x_2\ldots x_n}\notin\mathcal{N}$. Since $N|_{x_{n-n_2+1}\ldots x_n}\subset\mathcal{N}$, it follows that $g|_{x_1x_2\ldots x_{n-n_2}}\notin N$. Consequently, the projection $\gamma''$ of the path $\gamma'$ to a path in $\Gamma_{n-n_2, S}$ obtained by removing the suffixes of length $n_2$ is $N$-essential.

Let $\phi$ be an $N$-admissible function on $\Gamma_{n-n_2, S}$. Define $\tilde\phi$ on an edge $(s, x_1x_2\ldots x_n)$ of $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}}$ as the sums of values of $\phi$ along the corresponding path in $\Gamma_{n-n_2, S}$ of length at most $r$ starting in $x_1x_2\ldots x_{n-n_2}$ (giving $s$ as the product of the first labels of the edges). Then the sum of values of $\tilde\phi$ along $\gamma$ will be equal to the sum of values of $\phi$ along $\gamma''$. It follows that $\tilde\phi$ is admissible.

If an edge $(s, x_1x_2\ldots x_{n-n_2})$ of $\Gamma_{n-n_2, S}$ appears in the sum defining the value of $\tilde\phi$ for an edge $(s, z_1z_2\ldots z_n)$ of $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}}$, then $z_1z_2\ldots z_{n-n_2}$ is on distance at most $r$ from $x_1x_2\ldots x_{n-n_2}$ in $\Gamma_{n-n_2, S}$. It follows that a given edge of $\Gamma_{n-n_2, S}$ appears in these sums at most $D=\deg(\mathfrak{B})^{n_2}(1+|S|+\cdots+|S|^r)$ times. Using the inequality $(a_1+\cdots+a_k)^p\le k^{p-1}(a_1^p+\cdots a_k^p)$, we conclude that the sum of values of the $p$th powers of $\tilde\phi$ is not larger than $r^{p-1}D\sum\phi(e)^p$. Consequently, 
\[M_{\mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}, p}(n)\le r^{p-1}D M_{\mathcal{A}_S p}(n)\]
for all $n$, which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{pr:moduluschangealb}
Let $\mathcal{A}_\mathsf{X}, \mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{Y}}$ be the sets of admissible functions on the sets of vertices of graphs $\Gamma_n$ defined using different bases $\mathsf{X}$ and $\mathsf{Y}$ of $\mathfrak{B}$, then 
\[M_{p, \mathcal{A}_\mathsf{X}}(n)\asymp M_{p, \mathcal{A}_{\mathsf{Y}}}(n).\]
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
We identify the trees $\mathsf{X}^*$ and $\mathsf{Y}^*$ by the natural isomorphism mapping $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ to the unique representative in $\mathsf{Y}^*$ of the right orbit $v\cdot G$.
 Let $\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X}$  and $\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{Y}}$ be the corresponding nuclei. 
  
 By Proposition~\ref{pr:sumgeometric}, there exists a finite set $A\subset G$ such that if $h_1$ is the section of an element $g\in G$ in a word $v_1\in\mathsf{X}^*$ (for the standard action associated with $\mathsf{X}$), and $h_2$ is the section of $g$ in the corresponding word $v_2\in\mathsf{Y}^*$ (such that $v_2\in v_1\cdot G$), then there exist $f_1, f_2\in B$ such that $h_2=f_1^{-1}h_1f_2$.
 In particular, if the $\mathsf{X}$-section of $g$ in $v$ belongs to $\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X}$, then the $\mathsf{Y}$-section of $g$ in the corresponding word belongs to $B^{-1}\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X} B$. Note that this implies that $\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{Y}}\subset B^{-1}\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X} B$, since all sections in long enough words must belong to the nucleus. We may assume that $B$ contains the identity, so we also have $\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X}\subset B^{-1}\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X} B$.

Consequently, if a path $\gamma$ in $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X}\cup\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{Y}}}$ is such that the corresponding product of sections defined using $\mathsf{X}$ does not belong to $B^{-1}\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X} B$, then the product of the sections defined using $\mathsf{Y}$ does not belong to $\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{Y}}$. 

In other words, every path in $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X}\cup\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{Y}}$ that is $B^{-1}\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X} B$-essential in the sense of sections defined using $\mathsf{X}$ is $\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{Y}}$-essential in the sense of sections defined using $\mathsf{Y}$. 

Consequently, every $\mathcal{N}_{\mathsf{Y}}$-admissible function in the sense of sections defined by $\mathsf{Y}$ is $B^{-1}\mathcal{N}_\mathsf{X} B$-admissible in the sense of sections defined using $\mathsf{X}$. This, together with Proposition~\ref{pr:moduluschanginggenset}, finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:hatequivalent}
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the set of admissible functions $\mathsf{X}^n\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$. Then there exists $C$, not depending on $n$, such that $M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)\asymp M_{\widehat{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n)$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
We obviously have $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}\subset\mathcal{A}$. Consequently, $M_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n)\ge M_{\mathcal{A}, p}$. 

Let $\phi\in \mathcal{A}$. Consider the function $\psi(v)=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{N}^3}\phi(s(v))$. Then for every $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$ there exists $s\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $\hat\psi(v)=\psi(s(v))$. For any $s_1, s_2\in\mathcal{N}$, the set $\mathcal{N}^3s$ contains $1$, $s_1$ and $s_2s_1$, hence
\[\hat\psi(v)=\psi(s(v))=\sum_{h\in\mathcal{N}^2}\phi(hs(v))\ge \phi(v)+\phi(s_1(v))+\phi(s_2s_1(v)).\]

Consequently, for any essential vertex-path $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m$, we have $\hat\psi(v_i)\ge \phi(v_i)$ for $i=1, 2, \ldots, m-1$, and $\hat\psi(v_{m-2})\ge\phi(v_{m-2})+\phi(v_{m-1})+\phi(v_m)$. Consequently,
\[\hat\psi(v_1)+\hat\psi(v_i)+\cdots+\hat\psi(v_{m-2})\ge\phi(v_1)+\phi(v_2)+\cdots+\phi(v_m)>1.\]
It follows that $\psi\in\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$.

We have $(\psi(v))^p\le |\mathcal{N}^3|^{p-1}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{N}^3}(\phi(s(v))^p$, consequently,
\[\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}(\psi(v))^p\le |\mathcal{N}^3|^{p-1}\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{N}^3}(\phi(s(v))^p=|\mathcal{N}^3|^p\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}(\phi(v))^p,\]
hence $M_{\widehat{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n)\le |\mathcal{N}^3|^pM_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:productadmissible}
Let $\phi_1\colon\mathsf{X}^{n_1}\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ and $\phi_2\colon\mathsf{X}^{n_2}\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ belong to $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$. Then the function $\phi\colon\mathsf{X}^{n_1+n_2}\longrightarrow[0, \infty)$ given by $\phi(v_1v_2)=\phi_1(v_1)\phi_2(v_2)$ also belongs to $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let $u_1w_1, u_2w_2, \ldots, u_mw_m$ be an essential vertex-path in $\mathsf{X}^{n_1+n_2}$, where $u_i\in\mathsf{X}^{n_1}$ and $w_i\in\mathsf{X}^{n_2}$. Let $s_i\in\mathcal{N}$ be such that $s_i(u_iw_i)=u_{i+1}w_{i+1}$.

Set $k_0=1$, and define $k_{i+1}$ inductively, by the condition that $u_{k_i}, u_{k_1+1}, \ldots, u_{k_{i+1}}$ is the shortest almost essential beginning of the path $u_{k_i}, u_{k_i+1}, \ldots, u_m$, if it exists. Let $l$ be the maximal value for which $k_l$ is defined.

Consider one of the segments $u_{k_i}, \ldots, u_{k_{i+1}}$.
Let $k_i\le j<k_{i+1}$. We have
\[\hat\phi(u_jw_j)=\min_{s\in\mathcal{N}}\phi(s(u_jw_j))=\min_{s\in\mathcal{N}}\phi_1(s(u_j))\phi_2(s|_{u_j}(w_j))\ge\hat\phi_1(u_j)\min_{s\in\mathcal{N}}\phi_2(s|_{u_j}(w_j)).\]
Let $s\in\mathcal{N}$ be an element realizing the minimum $\min_{s\in\mathcal{N}}\phi_2(s|_{u_j}(w_j))$. By construction, the path $u_{k_i}, \ldots, u_j, s(u_j)$ is not essential, i.e., the section $h=(ss_j\cdots s_{k_i+1}s_{k_i})|_{u_{k_i}}$ belongs to the nucleus.

But we have $h(w_{k_i})=s|_{u_j}(w_j)$. Therefore, $\phi_2(s|_{u_j}(w_j))=\phi_2(h(w_{k_i}))\ge \hat\phi(w_{k_i})$.

We have shown that 
\[\hat\phi(u_jw_j)\ge \hat\phi_1(u_j)\hat\phi(w_{k_i}).\] 
                                                         
                                                         

Since the path $u_{k_i}, u_{k_i+1}, \ldots, u_{k_{i+1}}$ is almost essential, we can continue it by one edge to an essential path, so the definition of the class $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$ implies that
\[\sum_{j=k_i}^{k_{i+1}-1}\hat\phi(u_jw_j)\ge \hat\phi(w_{k_i})\sum_{j=k_i}^{k_{i+1}-1}\hat\phi(u_j)>\hat\phi(w_{k_i}).\]

Since the paths $u_{k_i}w_{k_i}, \ldots, u_{k_{i+1}}w_{k_{i+1}}$ are not essential, there exists $h\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $w_{k_{i+1}}=h(w_{k_i})$. Consequently, we get a path $w_1=w_{k_0}, w_{k_1}, w_{k_2}, \ldots, w_{k_l}, w_m$ in $\mathsf{X}^{n_2}$ with the same section as the original path in $\mathsf{X}^{n_1+n_2}$. Since the original path is essential, we have $\sum_{i=0}^{l-1}\hat\phi_2(w_{k_i})>1$ if $k_l\ne m$, and $\sum_{i=0}^{l-2}\hat\phi_2(w_{k_i})>1$ if $k_l=m$.

If $k_l\ne m$, then $k_l-1<k_l<m$, so $k_l-1\le m-2$, and
\[\sum_{i=1}^{m-2}\hat\phi(u_iw_k)\ge \sum_{i=0}^{l-1}\hat\phi(w_{k_i})>1.\]
If $k_l=m$, then $k_{l-1}-1<k_{l-1}<m$, so $k_{l-1}-1\le m-2$, and
\[\sum_{i=1}^{m-2}\hat\phi(u_iw_k)\ge \sum_{i=0}^{l-2}\hat\phi(w_{k_i})>1,\]
which shows that $\phi\in\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be one of the classes of admissible or strongly admissible functions, defined above.

The limits
\[\theta_p=\lim_{n\to\infty} M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)^{\frac 1{np}},\qquad\theta_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}M_{\mathcal{A}, \infty}(n)^{\frac 1n}\]
exist for every $p>0$ and do not depend on the choice of the class $\mathcal{A}$ defined above.

The inequality $\theta_p<1$ is equivalent to the condition $\lim_{n\to\infty} M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)=0$ and to the condition $\inf_n M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)=0$.
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let us prove the statement for finite $p$, the case $p=\infty$ is similar.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:hatequivalent}, it is enough to prove the proposition for the class $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$. 

Let $\phi_1, \phi_2, \phi$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:productadmissible}.

Since $\sum_{w\in\mathsf{X}^{n_1+n_2}}\phi(w)^p=\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^{n_1}}\phi_1(v)^p\sum_{u\in\mathsf{X}^{n_2}}\phi_2(u)^p$, Lemma~\ref{lem:productadmissible} implies the inequality we have \[M_{\widehat{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n_1+n_2)\le M_{\widehat{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n_1) M_{\widehat{\mathcal{A}}, p}(n_2),\]
which finishes the proof of our proposition by Fekete's lemma.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{pr:asympmodulus}
The asymptotic moduli satisfy, for all $1<p<q\le\infty$, the inequalities:
    \[\theta_p\ge \theta_q,\qquad \mathsf{D}^{-1/p}\theta_p\le \mathsf{D}^{-1/q}\theta_q,\]
    where $\mathsf{D}=|\mathfrak{B}/G|$.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Since $M_p(n)^{1/p}$ for $p\in (1, \infty)$ and $M_\infty(n)$ for $p=\infty$ are equal to the infimum of the $\ell^p$-norms of admissible functions $\phi\colon \mathsf{X}^n\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$, we get $M_p(n)^{1/p}\ge M_q(n)^{1/q}$ for all $1<p<q<\infty$ and $M_p(n)^{1/p}\le M_\infty(n)$ for all $1<p<\infty$. This implies the inequality $\theta_p\ge\theta_q$ for all $1<p<q\le\infty$.

In the other direction, H\"older's inequality for $\ell^p$-norms in $\mathbb{R}^m$, implies the inequality $M_p(n)^{1/p}\le \mathsf{D}^{n\left(\frac 1p-\frac 1q\right)}M_q(n)^{1/q}$ for all $1<p<q<\infty$ and $M_p(n)^{1/p}\le\mathsf{D}^{\frac np}$ for all $1<p<\infty$. Passing to the limit, we get the inequality $\mathsf{D}^{-1/p}\theta_p\le \mathsf{D}^{-1/q}\theta_q$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- example-11: body_md -->
\label{ex:Grigmodulus}
As we have seen above, a function on the set of edges of the dual Moore diagram of the adding machine group is strongly admissible if and only if the sum of its values is greater than or equal to $1$. It follows from the inequalities between generalized means that the $p$-modulus $M_p$ (for the class of strongly admissible functions) is realized by the constant function equal to $2^{-n}$. Consequently, $\theta_p=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{2^n}{2^{np}}\right)^{1/np}=2^{\frac 1p-1}$.
The same arguments show that the Grigorchuk group has the same value $\theta_p=2^{\frac 1p-1}$ of the asymptotic modulus as the binary adding machine.
<!-- end example-11 -->
<!-- example-12: body_md -->
\label{ex:thetapbasilica}
The dual Moore diagram for the action of the generators $a, b$ of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$ on $\{0, 1\}^6$ is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:basilicagraph}. Any two simple cycles of the diagram are either disjoint or intersect in a single vertex. There are only two arrows with non-trivial labels: one labeled by $a$ and one labeled by $b$. Both of them start at $11\ldots 1$. The nucleus of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$ is $\{1, a^{\pm 1}, b^{\pm 1}, (ab^{-1})^{\pm 1}\}$, see~\ref{ex:basilicanucleus}. Consequently, $M_p$ is realized on a constant function supported on two simple cycles containing the vertex $11\ldots 1$. The lengths of these cycles in a diagram of level $n$ are $2^{n/2}$ and $2^{n/2}$, if $n$ is even, and $2^{(n+1)/2}$ and $2^{(n-1)/2}$, if $n$ is odd. It follows that $\theta_p=(\sqrt{2})^{\frac 1p-1}$.
<!-- end example-12 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{th:modulus}
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a contracting self-similar group, let $\mathsf{X}\subset\mathfrak{B}$ be a basis.

If  $p>\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$, then $\theta_p(G, \mathfrak{B})<1$.

If $\theta_p<1$, then there exists $n\ge 1$, a positive $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism $\nu\colon \mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow (0, \infty)$ and a visual metric on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ associated with $\nu$ of Hausdorff dimension less than or equal to $p$. In particular, $\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})\le p$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Let us prove the first statement of the theorem.
By Proposition~\ref{pr:diamoftiles} there exist a metric  and a measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$, and a constant $C>1$ such that \[\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}_v)^\alpha\asymp_C \mu(\mathcal{T}_v)\] for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$. Consider the lifts of this metric and the measure $\mu$ to $\mathcal{X}_{G}$, as described in Subsection~\ref{ss:liftingmm}.

Then there exists $C_1>1$ such that
\[\mu(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)\asymp_{C_1}\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)^\alpha\]
for all $v\in\mathfrak{B}^*$.

Let $r_0>0$ be less than distance between any two tiles $\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}\cdot g$ for $g\notin\mathcal{N}$. It exists, since any such tiles are disjoint.

Define $\phi_n\colon \mathsf{X}^n\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ by $\phi_n(v)=\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)$. Consider an edge-path $\gamma=((s_1, v_1), (s_2, v_2), \ldots, (s_m, v_m))$ in $\Gamma_n$. Consider its lift to the graph of $\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n}$ starting in $v_1$. It passes through the vertices $u_1=v_1, u_2=s_1\cdot u_1, u_3=s_2\cdot u_2, \ldots, u_{m+1}=s_m\cdot u_m$. We have $u_{m+1}=(s_m\cdots s_1(v_1))\cdot (s_m\cdots s_1)|_{v_1}$. In particular, $\mathcal{T}\otimes v_1\subset\mathcal{T}$ and $\mathcal{T}\otimes u_m\subset\mathcal{T}\cdot (s_m\cdots s_1)|_{v_1}$. It follows that distance between any two points $\xi\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_1$ and $\zeta\in\mathcal{T}\otimes u_{m+1}$ is more than $r_0$, if $(s_m\cdots s_1)|_{v_1}\notin\mathcal{N}$.

On the other hand, since $u_i=v_i\cdot (s_{i-1}\cdots s_1)|_{v_1}$, we have $\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes u_i)=\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i)=\phi_n(v_i)$, so
 $d(\xi, \zeta)\le\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes u_i)=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\phi(v_i)$. 
 
 It follows that $r_0^{-1}\phi_n\colon \mathsf{X}^n\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is an admissible function. Let $p>\alpha$. Then $\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*}(\phi_n(v))^p\le\max_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}(\phi_n(v))^{p-\alpha}\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*}(\phi_n(v))^\alpha\le C_1\max_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}(\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v))^{p-\alpha}\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*}\mu(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)$ for some constant $C_1$. We have $\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*}\mu(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)\le|\mathcal{N}|\mu(\mathcal{T})$, since the sets $\mathcal{T}\otimes v$ for $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$ form a cover of $\mathcal{T}$ of multiplicity at most $|\mathcal{N}|$. Since $\max_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v)\le C_2\lambda^n$ for some $C_2>1$ and $\lambda_0\in (0, 1)$, see Proposition~\ref{pr:diamoftiles}, we conclude that $M_n(p)\le C_3(\lambda_0^{p-\alpha})^n$ for all $n$. Consequently, $\theta_p\le\lambda_0^{p-\alpha}<1$.


Let us prove the second statement of the theorem. The idea is, given $\theta_p<1$,  to construct  a $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism such that the associated visual metric of exponent $1$ exists and has Haudorff dimension equal to an arbitrary number greater than $p$, using the following proposition.

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:exponetiated}
Let $\nu\colon\mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ be a $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism. 

Suppose that for every path $(s_{m-1}, x_{m-1}v_{m-1}), \ldots, (s_2, x_2v_2), (s_1, x_1v_1)$ in $\Gamma_n$, where $x_i\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v_i\in\mathsf{X}^{n-1}$, such that the path $(s_{m-1}\cdots s_2s_1)|_{x_1}\ne\mathcal{N}$, we have
\[e^{-\nu(x_1v_1)}+e^{-\nu(x_2v_2)}+\cdots+e^{-\nu(x_{m-2}v_{m-2})}>e^{-\nu(v_1)}\]
and
\[e^{-\nu(x_2v_2)}+e^{-\nu(x_3v_3)}+\cdots+e^{-\nu(x_{m-1}v_{m-1})}>e^{-\nu(v_i)}\]
for all $i=2, 3, \ldots, m-1$.

Then there exists a visual metric $d_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ of exponent $1$.
\end{proposition}


\begin{proof}
Let us denote $\delta(v)=e^{-\nu(v)}$.

We say that a sequence $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\in\mathsf{X}^*$ is a \emph{chain} if $\mathcal{T}_{v_i}\cap\mathcal{T}_{v_{i+1}}$ for all $i=1, \ldots, m-1$. Its \emph{mass} is the sum $\delta(v_1)+\delta(v_2)+\cdots+\delta(v_m)$. Its \emph{length} is $m$. We say that the chain \emph{connects} points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ if $\xi_1\in\mathcal{T}_{v_1}$ and $\xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{v_m}$.

Define $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ as the infimum of masses of all chains connecting $\xi_1$ to $\xi_2$. The function $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ is symmetric, satisfies the triangle ineaquality, and $d(\xi, \xi)=0$ for all $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$. Therefore, the proof of the proposition will be complete, if we show that $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$.

We may consider, in the definition of $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$, only chains without repetitions, since otherwise, we can remove a segment of the chain between the repetitions, and get a chain of smaller mass and length, connecting the same points.

Let $u=x_k\ldots x_2x_1$ and $v=y_l\ldots y_2y_1$ for $k\ge l$. 
Suppose that $x_1v_1, x_2v_2, \ldots, x_mv_m\in\mathsf{X}^n$ is a chain consisting of words of equal lengths, where $x_i\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v_i\in\mathsf{X}^{n-1}$. Let $s_i\in\mathcal{N}$ be such that $s_i(x_iv_i)=x_{i+1}v_{i+1}$. We get a path $(s_{m-1}, x_{m-1}v_{m-1}), \ldots, (s_2, x_2v_2), (s_1, x_1v_1)$ in $\Gamma_n$.

Similarly to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:productadmissible}, find a sequence $k_0=1<k_1<k_2<\ldots<k_l\le m$ such that each path $(s_{k_{i+1}-1}, x_{k_{i+1}-1}), \ldots, (s_{k_{i+1}}, x_{k_i+1}), (s_{k_i}, x_{k_i})$ from $x_{k_i}$ to $x_{k_{i+1}}$ in $\Gamma_1$ is almost essential but not essential. The last segment connecting $x_{k_l}$ to $x_m$ is not almost essential, if $k_l<m$.

By the condition of the proposition, we have
\[\delta(x_{k_i}v_{k_i})+\delta(x_{k_i+1}v_{k_i+1})+\cdots+\delta(x_{k_{i+1}-1}v_{k_{i+1}-1})>\delta(v_{k_i}).\]

Note that the path from $x_{k_i}$ to $x_{k_{i+1}}$ is not essential (if it is, then the path obtained by removing the last vertex is almost essential), i.e., 
$(s_{k_{i+1}}\cdots s_{k_i+1}s_{k_i})|_{x_{k_i}}\in\mathcal{N}$. We have $(s_{k_{i+1}}\cdots s_{k_i+1}s_{k_i})|_{x_{k_i}}(v_{k_i})=v_{k_{i+1}}$, hence $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_i}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_{i+1}}}$ are adjacent. Note that $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_i}}\supset \mathcal{T}_{x_{k_i}v_{k_i}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_{i+1}}}\supset \mathcal{T}_{x_{k_{i+1}}v_{k_{i+1}}}$

We see that if we replace in the the chain $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_mv_m$ the initial segment $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_{k_{l-1}}v_{k_{l-1}}$ by $v_1, v_{k_1}, \ldots, v_{k_{l-1}}$, we get a chain of smaller mass and length. All paths $(s_j, x_j), \ldots, (s_{k_{l-1}+1}, x_{k_{l-1}+1}, (s_{k_{l-1}}, x_{k_{l-1}})$ for $k_{l-1}\le j<k_l$, and all paths $(s_j, x_j), \ldots, (s_{k_l+1}, x_{k_l+1}), (s_{k_l}, x_{k_l})$ for $k_l\le j<m$ are not essential.
It follows that $x_jv_j\in\mathsf{X}\cdot \mathcal{N}(v_{k_{l-1}})$ for $k_{l-1}\le j<k_l$ and $x_jv_j\in\mathsf{X}\cdot\mathcal{N}(v_{k_l})$ for $k_l\le j<m$.

Since we assume that the chain has no repetitions, the length of the segment $x_{k_{l-1}+1}v_{k_{l-1}+1}, \ldots, x_mv_m$ is less than $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$.
Consequently, we may consider only chains such that the length of its segments consisting of words of constant length is at most $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$.

Suppose now that we have a chain $v_0, x_1v_1, \ldots, x_mv_m, v_{m+1}$, where $|v_1|=|v_2|=\ldots=|v_m|=n$ and $|v_0|, |v_{m+1}|\le n$. Then there exist elements $s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_m\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $s_i(x_iv_i)=x_{i+1}v_{i+1}$ for $i=1, 2, \ldots, m$, the word $v_{m+1}$ is a suffix of $s_m(x_mv_m)$, and $v_0$ is a suffix of $s_0^{-1}(x_1v_1)$, see Lemma~\ref{lem:intersectingtiles}. Let $x_0, x_{m+1}\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v_0', v_{m+1}'\in\mathsf{X}^n$ be such that $x_0v_0'=s_0^{-1}(x_1v_1)$ and $x_{m+1}v_{m+1}'=s_m(x_mv_m)$. Then $v_0$ and $v_{m+1}$ are suffixes of $v_0'$ and $v_{m+1}'$, respectively.

If the path $(s_m, x_m), \ldots (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ is not essential, then $s(v_0')=v_{m+1}'$ for $s=(s_m\cdots s_1s_0)|_{x_0}\in\mathcal{N}$, hence $\mathcal{T}_{v_0}\cap \mathcal{T}_{v_{m+1}}\ne\emptyset$, so we can delete the segment $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_mv_m$ from the chain, and get a shorter chain of smaller mass, connecting the same points.

Suppose that the path $(s_m, x_m), \ldots, (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ is essential. Find its shortest almost essential beginning $(s_{k-1}, x_{k-1}), \ldots, (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ connecting $x_0$ to $x_k$ for $k\le m$. Let $(s, x_k), (s_{k-1}, x_{k-1}), \ldots, (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ be its essential continuation by one edge. Then, by the condition of the proposition, we have 
\[\delta(v_k)<\delta(x_1v_1)+\delta(x_2v_2)+\cdots+\delta(x_kv_k).\]
Since the path from $x_0$ to $x_k$ is not essential, the tiles $\mathcal{T}_{v_0'}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_k}$ intersect, henc $\mathcal{T}_{v_0}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_k}$ intersect. We can replace the segment $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_kv_k$ by $v_k$, and get a shorter chain of smaller mass. 

Thus, we can shorten the chain to get a chain of smaller mass in both cases. 
It follows that $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ is equal to the infimum of the masses of chains connecting $\xi_1$ to $\xi_2$ such that the segments of the chain consisting of words of constant length have at most $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$ elements and 
are not adjacent to two shorter words.

Suppose that $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m$ is such a chain. Let $l$ be an index such that $|v_l|$ is minimal. Then $|v_i|$ is non-increasing for $i\le l$ and non-decreasing for $i\ge l$. It follows that there exist $s_i, r_i\in\mathcal{N}$ and $u_i\in\mathsf{X}^*$ such that if  $v_{i-1}=s_i(u_iv_i)$ for all $i\le l$, and $v_{i+1}=r_i(u_iv_i)$ for all $i\ge l$. Therefore,
\begin{align*}v_1&=s_2\left(u_2 s_3\left(u_3\ldots s_l\left(u_lv_l\right)\ldots \right)\right)\\
v_m&=r_{m-1}\left(u_{m-1}r_{m-2}\left(u_{m-2}\ldots r_l\left(u_lv_l\right)\ldots\right)\right),
\end{align*}
where no more than $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$ of consecutive words in the sequence $u_i$ can be empty.

Applying Proposition~\ref{pr:sumgeometric} to the set $A=\mathcal{N}^{2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|}$, we find a finite set $\mathcal{N}_A$, depending only on $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathsf{X}$ such that the above equalities imply
\[v_1=w_1 h_1(v_l),\qquad v_m=w_2 h_2(v_l),\]
for some $w_i\in\mathsf{X}^*$ and $h_1, h_2\in\mathcal{N}_A$. 
The element $h_2h_1^{-1}$ maps the suffix $h_1(v_l)$ of $v_1$ to the suffix $h_2(v_l)$ of $v_m$.

Let $t$ be such that $(\mathcal{N}_A\cdot \mathcal{N}_A^{-1})|_{\mathsf{X}^t}\subset\mathcal{N}$, and let $v_1', v_m'$ be the suffixes of $v_1, v_m$, respectively, of length $|v_l|-t$. Then there is an element of the nucleus mapping $v_1'$ to $v_m'$. We have $\mathcal{T}_{v_1'}\supset \mathcal{T}_{v_1}$, $\mathcal{T}_{v_m'}\supset\mathcal{T}_{v_m}$, and $\mathcal{T}_{v_1'}\cap\mathcal{T}_{v_2'}\ne\emptyset$. We get a chain connecting $\xi_1$ to $\xi_2$ of mass $\delta(v_1')+\delta(v_2')$. Since $\nu$ is a $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism, and $v_i'$ are images of suffixes of length $|v_l|-t$ of $v_l$ under elements of $\mathcal{N}$, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that $\delta(v_i')\le C_1\delta(v_l)$. 

Since $\xi_1\in\mathcal{T}_{v_1}\subset\mathcal{T}_{v_1'}$ and $\xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{v_m}\subset\mathcal{T}_{v_m'}$, the points $\xi_1, \xi_2$ can be represented by left-infinite sequences with suffixes $v_1'$ and $v_m'$, respectively. Since they are images of each other under the action of elements of the nucleus, $\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)\ge\nu(v_1')-C$ for some constant $C_2\ge 0$.


The mass of the original chain $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ is greater or equal to $\delta(v_l)\ge C_1^{-1}(\delta(v_1')+\delta(v_2'))\ge C_1\delta(v_1')\ge C_3e^{-\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$, which finishes the proof.
\end{proof}


After passing to an iterate $(G, \mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n})$, we may assume that the basis $\mathsf{X}$ is such that $(\mathcal{N}^2)|_{\mathsf{X}}=\mathcal{N}$.

Consider the class $\mathcal{B}$  of functions $\phi\colon\mathsf{X}^n\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ satisfying the following condition. For every essential path in $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}}$ passing through vertices $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m$, we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Lhcond1}
\hat\phi(v_1)+\hat\phi(v_2)+\cdots+\hat\phi(v_{m-2})>1
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:Lhcond2}
\hat\phi(v_2)+\hat\phi(v_3)+\cdots+\hat\phi(v_{m-1})>1,
\end{equation}
where, as before, $\hat\phi(v)=\min_{s\in\mathcal{N}}\phi(s(v))$.

By the same arguments as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:hatequivalent}, we have $M_{\mathcal{B}, p}(n)\asymp M_{\mathcal{A}, p}(n)$ for the class $\mathcal{A}$ of admissible functions.

Assume that $\theta_p<1$. Then $M_{\mathcal{B}, p}(n)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$.
Let $\lambda_0$ be a small positive number, which we will choose later. Let $n_0$ be such that $M_{\mathcal{B}, p}(n)<\lambda_0$. Let us pass to  $\mathsf{X}^{n_0}$, so that we have $M_{\mathcal{B}, p}(1)<\lambda_0$. 
Let $\phi\in\mathcal{B}$ be such that $\sum_{x\in\mathsf{X}}\phi(x)^p<\lambda_0$.

Note that it follows that $\phi(x)\in [0, 1)$ for every $x\in\mathsf{X}$. By adding a small constant $\epsilon$ to $\phi$, we may assume that $0<\eta_-\le\phi(x)\le\eta_+<1$ for some constants $\eta_-, \eta_+$ and $\sum_{x\in\mathsf{X}}\phi(x)^p\le 2\lambda_0<1$. (Provided $\lambda_0<1/2$.)

Consider the metric on the self-similarity complex $\Sigma$ defined by the following lengths of the generators of $\mathfrak{B}$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\|x\|=-\log\phi(x)$ for $x\in\mathsf{X}$,
    \item $\|s\|=M$ for $s\in\mathcal{N}$, where $M>2\max\{\|x\|\colon x\in\mathsf{X}\}$.
\end{itemize}
