Let $\Sigma_\phi$ be the obtained metric graph.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                         

The original lengths of paths and distances in $\Sigma$ will be called \emph{combinatorial}.

\begin{lemma}
\label{lem:geodesicsinSigmaphi}
A geodesic path in $\Sigma_\phi$ can not have more than two consecutive horizontal edges, and it has all descending edges appearing before all the ascending ones
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Consider a horizontal path of length $kM$ starting in a vertex $xv\in\mathsf{X}^*$ for $x\in\mathsf{X}$ and corresponding to the word $s_k\cdots s_2s_1$ of elements of $\mathcal{N}$. Then $v$ and $(s_k\cdots s_2s_1)|_x(v)$ can be connected by a horizontal path $\gamma$ of combinatorial length at most $\lceil k/2\rceil$. If $k>1$, then $\lceil k/2\rceil\le k-1$. Then the path consisting of the descending edge $(xv, v)$, followed by the path $\gamma$ and then by the ascending edge from $(s_k\cdots s_2s_1)|_x(v)$ to $(s_k\cdots s_2s_1)(v)$ has length less than $M/2+(k-1)M+M/2=kM$, so $\gamma$ is not a geodesic path in $\Sigma_\phi$. This shows that a geodesic path in $\Sigma_\phi$ can not have two consecutive horizontal edges.

A path consisting of an ascending edge $(v, xv)$, horizontal edge $(xv, s(xv))$, and a descending edge $(s(xv), s|_x(v))$ has length $\|x\|+M+\|s(x)\|>M$. But there is a horizontal edge from $v$ to $s|_x(v)$ (or these vertices coincide), which shows that we can not have an ascending edge before a descending edge in a geodesic in $\Sigma_\phi$.
\end{proof}

Denote by $\nu(v)$, for $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$, be the distance in $\Sigma_\phi$ from $v$ to $\emptyset$.

\begin{lemma}
    The function $\nu\colon \mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow (0, \infty)$ is a positive $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism.
\end{lemma}


\begin{proof}
Positivity of $\nu$ follows from the fact that $\Sigma_\phi$ is quasi-isometric to $\Sigma$. For every $g\in\mathcal{N}$ we have $|\nu(v)-\nu(g(v))|\le\|s\|=M$, by the triangle inequality, hence $\nu$ is $G$-quasi-invariant.

For every $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$, the geodesic paths from $\emptyset$ to $v$ in $\Sigma_\phi$ contains only ascending or horizontal edges, since, by Lemma~\ref{lem:geodesicsinSigmaphi}, in any geodesic path all descending edges come before the ascending ones, but there are no descending or horizontal edges starting in $\emptyset$.

Let $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$, and $\gamma$ be the geodesic paths starting in $\emptyset$ and ending in $v_1, v_2, v_1v_2$ for some $v_1, v_2\in\mathsf{X}^*$. Since all edges of these paths are ascending or horizontal, the labels read along them belong to $\mathsf{X}\cup\mathcal{N}$, and no consecutive labels belong to $\mathcal{N}$. Let $\overline w_1, \overline w_2, \overline w$ be the corresponding words in $\mathsf{X}\cup\mathcal{N}$, and let $w_1, w_2, w\in\mathfrak{B}^*$ be the corresponding products of the generators of the semigroup $\mathfrak{B}^*$. We obtain $w_1(\emptyset)=v_1, w_2(\emptyset)=v_2, w(\emptyset)=v_1v_2$. Since $\mathcal{N}^2|_\alpha=\mathcal{N}$ and no two consecutive generators in the wors $\overline w_i, \overline w$ belong to $\mathcal{N}$, we get that $w_1=v_1\cdot h_1, w_2=v_2\cdot h_2$, and $w=v_1v_2\cdot h_3$ for some $h_i\in\mathcal{N}^2$.

Let $\gamma_1'$ be the path starting in $h_1^{-1}(v_2)$ and labeled by the same labels as $\gamma_1$. Then it will end in $w_1h_1^{-1}(v_2)=v_1h_1h_1^{-1}(v_2)=v_1v_2$. Since the labels of $\gamma_1'$ and $\gamma_1$ are the same, there lengths are equal. Consequently,
\[\nu(v_1v_2)\le d(v_1v_2, h_1^{-1}(v_2))+d(h_1^{-1}(v_2), v_2)+d(v_2, \emptyset)\le \nu(v_1)+\nu(v_2)+2M.\]

Let $w_1'$ be the beginning of $\overline w$ (seen as an element of $\mathfrak{B}^*$) such that $w_1'\in\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes |v_1|}$. Let $w_2'$ be the rest of $w$, so that $w=w_1'w_2'$. Since $w=v_1v_2\cdot h_3$, and there are no two consecutive elements of $\mathcal{N}$ in $\overline w$, we have, for some $h_1'\in\mathcal{N}^2$, that $w_1'=v_1\cdot h_1'$. We have $v_1v_2\cdot h_3=v_1\cdot h_1'\cdot (h_1')^{-1}v_2\cdot h_3$. Consequently, $v_2'=(h_1')^{-1}v_2$ is a vertex of $\gamma$ splitting it into a path from $\emptyset$ to $v_2'$ labeled by $w_2'=(h_1')^{-1}v_2\cdot h_3$ and the path from $v_2'$ to $v_1v_2$ labeled by $w_1'=v_1\cdot h_1'$. The length of the first path is greater or equal to the distance from $\emptyset$ to $v_2$ minus $|v_2-(h_1')^{-1}(v_2)|\le 2M$. The length of the second path is the same as the length of the path with the same labels connecting $\emptyset$ to $w_1'(\emptyset)=v_1$, which is greater or equal to $\nu(v_1)$. Consequently,
\[\nu(v_1v_2)\ge \nu(v_2)-2M+\nu(v_1),\]
which finishes the proof that $\nu$ is a quasi-morphism.
\end{proof}

It follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:geodesicsinSigmaphi} that a geodesic path in $\Sigma_\phi$ from $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ to $\emptyset$ either starts with a descending edge, or with a horizontal edge followed by a descending edge. Consequently, for every $xv\in\mathsf{X}^*$ there exists $s\in\mathcal{N}$ such that the word $yu=s(xv)$ satisfies     
\[\nu(yu)=-\log(\phi(y))+\nu(u).\]
Note that it follows from the triangle inequality that
\[\nu(xv)\le-\log(\phi(x))+\nu(v)\]
for all $x\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$.


Denote $\delta(v)=e^{-\nu(v)}$. Since $\nu$ is $G$-quasi-invariant, we have $\delta\asymp\hat\delta$.
Let us show that $\hat\delta$ satisfies the conditions of Proposition~\ref{prop:exponetiated}, which will show that there exists a metric $d$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ such that $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$. Consider a path \[(s_{m-1}, x_{m-1}v_{m-1}), \ldots, (s_2, x_2v_2), (s_1, x_1v_1)\] in $\Gamma_{n, \mathcal{N}}$ connecting $x_1v_1$ to $x_mv_m$, where $x_i\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v_i\in\mathsf{X}^{n-1}$, such that the path $(s_{m-1}\cdots s_2s_1)|_{x_1}\notin\mathcal{N}$, as in the conditions of Proposition~\ref{prop:exponetiated}.

Let us prove the first inequality
\[\hat\delta(x_1v_1)+\hat\delta(x_2v_2)+\cdots+\hat\delta(x_{m-2}v_{m-2})>\hat\delta(v_1).\]

Let $(s_{k-1}, x_{k-1}), \ldots, (s_2, x_2), (s_1, x_1)$
be the shortest almost essential beginning of the path. It connects $x_1$ to $x_k$. We have $k<m$, since the path for $k=m-1$ is almost essential.

Let $1\le i\le k-1$, and let $h_i\in\mathcal{N}$ be such that $\hat\delta(x_iv_i)=\delta(h_i(x_iv_i))$. Since the beginning of the path connecting $x_1$ to $x_iv_i$ is not almost essential, the section $s=(h_is_i\cdots s_1)|_{x_1}$ belongs to the nucleus, hence we have
\[\hat\delta(x_iv_i)=\delta(h_i(x_iv_i))\ge\phi(h_i(x_i))\delta(s(v_1))\ge\hat\phi(x_i)\hat\delta(v_1).\]

Consider a continuation \[(s, x_k),  (s_{k-1}, x_{k-1}), \ldots, (s_2, x_2), (s_1, x_1)\] of the path to an essential path.

Then $\phi\in\mathcal{B}$ implies that
\begin{multline*}
\hat\delta(x_1v_1)+\hat\delta(x_2v_2)+\cdots+\hat\delta(x_{m-2}v_{m-2})\ge \\
\hat\delta(x_1v_1)+\hat\delta(x_2v_2)+\cdots+\hat\delta(x_{k-1}v_{k-1})\ge\\
\left(\hat\phi(x_1)+\hat\phi(v_2)+\cdots+\hat\phi(x_{k-1})\right)\hat\delta(v_1)>\delta(v_1).
\end{multline*}

Let us prove the second inequality of Proposition~\ref{prop:exponetiated}. Choose $j\in\{2, 3, \ldots, m-1\}$. If there is an almost essential path
\[(s_j, x_j), (s_{j+1}, x_{j+1}), \ldots\]
or an almost essential path
\[(s_{j-1}^{-1}, x_j), (s_{j-2}^{-1}, x_{j-1}), \ldots\] going in the opposite direction, then the same argument as above will finish the proof. If all such paths are not almost essential, then the same arguments as above show that $\hat\delta(x_iv_i)\ge\hat\phi(x_i)\hat\delta(v_j)$ for all $j$, hence
\begin{multline*}
\hat\delta(x_2v_2)+\hat\delta(x_3v_3)+\cdots+\hat\delta(x_{m-1}v_{m-1})\ge\\
\left(\hat\phi(x_2)+\hat\phi(x_3)+\cdots+\hat\phi(x_{m-1})\right)\hat\delta(x_j)>\delta(x_j).
\end{multline*}

Consequently, the function $\hat\delta$ satisfies the conditions of Proposition~\ref{prop:exponetiated}, hence there exists a visual metric associated with $\nu$ of exponent $1$.



\begin{lemma}
For any $x\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ there exists $s\in\mathcal{N}$ such that 
\[\nu(xv)-\nu(v)\ge -\log\phi(s(x)).\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If the geodesic path from $xv$ to $\emptyset$  starts with the vertical edge $(xv, v)$, then
\[\nu(xv)=-\log\phi(x)+\nu(v).\]

Suppose that it starts with a horizontal edge $(xv, s(xv))$ for some $s$. Since we can not have two consecutive horizontal edges, the next edge of the geodesic path is the vertical edge $(s(xv), s|_x(v))$, hence
\[\nu(xv)=M-\log\phi(s(x))+\nu(s|_x(v)).\]
We have a horizontal edge $(v, s|_x(v))$, hence, by triangle inequality,
\[\nu(v)\le M+\nu(s|_x(v)).\]
It follows that
\[\nu(xv)-\nu(v)\ge -\log\phi(s(x)),\]
which finishes the proof.
\end{proof}

It follows that for every $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ we have
\begin{multline*}
\sum_{x\in\mathsf{X}}e^{-p(\nu(xv)-\nu(v))}\le\sum_{x\in\mathsf{X}}e^{p\log\phi(s_x(x))}\\
=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{X}}\phi(s_x(x))^p\le|\mathcal{N}|\sum_{x\in\mathsf{X}}\phi(x)^p<2|\mathcal{N}|\lambda_0,
\end{multline*}
for some $s_x\in\mathcal{N}$.

By Proposition~\ref{pr:entropycriterion}, the $\nu$-entropy is less than or equal to $p$, if $\lambda_0<2|\mathcal{N}|^{-1}$. Since there is a visual metric associated with $\nu$ of exponent $1$, we get the inequality $\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})\le p$, finishing the proof.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop:exponetiated}
Let $\nu\colon\mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow [0, \infty)$ be a $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism. 

Suppose that for every path $(s_{m-1}, x_{m-1}v_{m-1}), \ldots, (s_2, x_2v_2), (s_1, x_1v_1)$ in $\Gamma_n$, where $x_i\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v_i\in\mathsf{X}^{n-1}$, such that the path $(s_{m-1}\cdots s_2s_1)|_{x_1}\ne\mathcal{N}$, we have
\[e^{-\nu(x_1v_1)}+e^{-\nu(x_2v_2)}+\cdots+e^{-\nu(x_{m-2}v_{m-2})}>e^{-\nu(v_1)}\]
and
\[e^{-\nu(x_2v_2)}+e^{-\nu(x_3v_3)}+\cdots+e^{-\nu(x_{m-1}v_{m-1})}>e^{-\nu(v_i)}\]
for all $i=2, 3, \ldots, m-1$.

Then there exists a visual metric $d_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$ on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ of exponent $1$.
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let us denote $\delta(v)=e^{-\nu(v)}$.

We say that a sequence $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\in\mathsf{X}^*$ is a \emph{chain} if $\mathcal{T}_{v_i}\cap\mathcal{T}_{v_{i+1}}$ for all $i=1, \ldots, m-1$. Its \emph{mass} is the sum $\delta(v_1)+\delta(v_2)+\cdots+\delta(v_m)$. Its \emph{length} is $m$. We say that the chain \emph{connects} points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$ if $\xi_1\in\mathcal{T}_{v_1}$ and $\xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{v_m}$.

Define $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ as the infimum of masses of all chains connecting $\xi_1$ to $\xi_2$. The function $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ is symmetric, satisfies the triangle ineaquality, and $d(\xi, \xi)=0$ for all $\xi\in\mathcal{J}_{G}$. Therefore, the proof of the proposition will be complete, if we show that $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{-\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$.

We may consider, in the definition of $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$, only chains without repetitions, since otherwise, we can remove a segment of the chain between the repetitions, and get a chain of smaller mass and length, connecting the same points.

Let $u=x_k\ldots x_2x_1$ and $v=y_l\ldots y_2y_1$ for $k\ge l$. 
Suppose that $x_1v_1, x_2v_2, \ldots, x_mv_m\in\mathsf{X}^n$ is a chain consisting of words of equal lengths, where $x_i\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v_i\in\mathsf{X}^{n-1}$. Let $s_i\in\mathcal{N}$ be such that $s_i(x_iv_i)=x_{i+1}v_{i+1}$. We get a path $(s_{m-1}, x_{m-1}v_{m-1}), \ldots, (s_2, x_2v_2), (s_1, x_1v_1)$ in $\Gamma_n$.

Similarly to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:productadmissible}, find a sequence $k_0=1<k_1<k_2<\ldots<k_l\le m$ such that each path $(s_{k_{i+1}-1}, x_{k_{i+1}-1}), \ldots, (s_{k_{i+1}}, x_{k_i+1}), (s_{k_i}, x_{k_i})$ from $x_{k_i}$ to $x_{k_{i+1}}$ in $\Gamma_1$ is almost essential but not essential. The last segment connecting $x_{k_l}$ to $x_m$ is not almost essential, if $k_l<m$.

By the condition of the proposition, we have
\[\delta(x_{k_i}v_{k_i})+\delta(x_{k_i+1}v_{k_i+1})+\cdots+\delta(x_{k_{i+1}-1}v_{k_{i+1}-1})>\delta(v_{k_i}).\]

Note that the path from $x_{k_i}$ to $x_{k_{i+1}}$ is not essential (if it is, then the path obtained by removing the last vertex is almost essential), i.e., 
$(s_{k_{i+1}}\cdots s_{k_i+1}s_{k_i})|_{x_{k_i}}\in\mathcal{N}$. We have $(s_{k_{i+1}}\cdots s_{k_i+1}s_{k_i})|_{x_{k_i}}(v_{k_i})=v_{k_{i+1}}$, hence $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_i}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_{i+1}}}$ are adjacent. Note that $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_i}}\supset \mathcal{T}_{x_{k_i}v_{k_i}}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_{k_{i+1}}}\supset \mathcal{T}_{x_{k_{i+1}}v_{k_{i+1}}}$

We see that if we replace in the the chain $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_mv_m$ the initial segment $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_{k_{l-1}}v_{k_{l-1}}$ by $v_1, v_{k_1}, \ldots, v_{k_{l-1}}$, we get a chain of smaller mass and length. All paths $(s_j, x_j), \ldots, (s_{k_{l-1}+1}, x_{k_{l-1}+1}, (s_{k_{l-1}}, x_{k_{l-1}})$ for $k_{l-1}\le j<k_l$, and all paths $(s_j, x_j), \ldots, (s_{k_l+1}, x_{k_l+1}), (s_{k_l}, x_{k_l})$ for $k_l\le j<m$ are not essential.
It follows that $x_jv_j\in\mathsf{X}\cdot \mathcal{N}(v_{k_{l-1}})$ for $k_{l-1}\le j<k_l$ and $x_jv_j\in\mathsf{X}\cdot\mathcal{N}(v_{k_l})$ for $k_l\le j<m$.

Since we assume that the chain has no repetitions, the length of the segment $x_{k_{l-1}+1}v_{k_{l-1}+1}, \ldots, x_mv_m$ is less than $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$.
Consequently, we may consider only chains such that the length of its segments consisting of words of constant length is at most $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$.

Suppose now that we have a chain $v_0, x_1v_1, \ldots, x_mv_m, v_{m+1}$, where $|v_1|=|v_2|=\ldots=|v_m|=n$ and $|v_0|, |v_{m+1}|\le n$. Then there exist elements $s_0, s_1, \ldots, s_m\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $s_i(x_iv_i)=x_{i+1}v_{i+1}$ for $i=1, 2, \ldots, m$, the word $v_{m+1}$ is a suffix of $s_m(x_mv_m)$, and $v_0$ is a suffix of $s_0^{-1}(x_1v_1)$, see Lemma~\ref{lem:intersectingtiles}. Let $x_0, x_{m+1}\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v_0', v_{m+1}'\in\mathsf{X}^n$ be such that $x_0v_0'=s_0^{-1}(x_1v_1)$ and $x_{m+1}v_{m+1}'=s_m(x_mv_m)$. Then $v_0$ and $v_{m+1}$ are suffixes of $v_0'$ and $v_{m+1}'$, respectively.

If the path $(s_m, x_m), \ldots (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ is not essential, then $s(v_0')=v_{m+1}'$ for $s=(s_m\cdots s_1s_0)|_{x_0}\in\mathcal{N}$, hence $\mathcal{T}_{v_0}\cap \mathcal{T}_{v_{m+1}}\ne\emptyset$, so we can delete the segment $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_mv_m$ from the chain, and get a shorter chain of smaller mass, connecting the same points.

Suppose that the path $(s_m, x_m), \ldots, (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ is essential. Find its shortest almost essential beginning $(s_{k-1}, x_{k-1}), \ldots, (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ connecting $x_0$ to $x_k$ for $k\le m$. Let $(s, x_k), (s_{k-1}, x_{k-1}), \ldots, (s_1, x_1), (s_0, x_0)$ be its essential continuation by one edge. Then, by the condition of the proposition, we have 
\[\delta(v_k)<\delta(x_1v_1)+\delta(x_2v_2)+\cdots+\delta(x_kv_k).\]
Since the path from $x_0$ to $x_k$ is not essential, the tiles $\mathcal{T}_{v_0'}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_k}$ intersect, henc $\mathcal{T}_{v_0}$ and $\mathcal{T}_{v_k}$ intersect. We can replace the segment $x_1v_1, \ldots, x_kv_k$ by $v_k$, and get a shorter chain of smaller mass. 

Thus, we can shorten the chain to get a chain of smaller mass in both cases. 
It follows that $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)$ is equal to the infimum of the masses of chains connecting $\xi_1$ to $\xi_2$ such that the segments of the chain consisting of words of constant length have at most $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$ elements and 
are not adjacent to two shorter words.

Suppose that $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m$ is such a chain. Let $l$ be an index such that $|v_l|$ is minimal. Then $|v_i|$ is non-increasing for $i\le l$ and non-decreasing for $i\ge l$. It follows that there exist $s_i, r_i\in\mathcal{N}$ and $u_i\in\mathsf{X}^*$ such that if  $v_{i-1}=s_i(u_iv_i)$ for all $i\le l$, and $v_{i+1}=r_i(u_iv_i)$ for all $i\ge l$. Therefore,
\begin{align*}v_1&=s_2\left(u_2 s_3\left(u_3\ldots s_l\left(u_lv_l\right)\ldots \right)\right)\\
v_m&=r_{m-1}\left(u_{m-1}r_{m-2}\left(u_{m-2}\ldots r_l\left(u_lv_l\right)\ldots\right)\right),
\end{align*}
where no more than $2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|$ of consecutive words in the sequence $u_i$ can be empty.

Applying Proposition~\ref{pr:sumgeometric} to the set $A=\mathcal{N}^{2|\mathsf{X}|\cdot|\mathcal{N}|}$, we find a finite set $\mathcal{N}_A$, depending only on $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ and $\mathsf{X}$ such that the above equalities imply
\[v_1=w_1 h_1(v_l),\qquad v_m=w_2 h_2(v_l),\]
for some $w_i\in\mathsf{X}^*$ and $h_1, h_2\in\mathcal{N}_A$. 
The element $h_2h_1^{-1}$ maps the suffix $h_1(v_l)$ of $v_1$ to the suffix $h_2(v_l)$ of $v_m$.

Let $t$ be such that $(\mathcal{N}_A\cdot \mathcal{N}_A^{-1})|_{\mathsf{X}^t}\subset\mathcal{N}$, and let $v_1', v_m'$ be the suffixes of $v_1, v_m$, respectively, of length $|v_l|-t$. Then there is an element of the nucleus mapping $v_1'$ to $v_m'$. We have $\mathcal{T}_{v_1'}\supset \mathcal{T}_{v_1}$, $\mathcal{T}_{v_m'}\supset\mathcal{T}_{v_m}$, and $\mathcal{T}_{v_1'}\cap\mathcal{T}_{v_2'}\ne\emptyset$. We get a chain connecting $\xi_1$ to $\xi_2$ of mass $\delta(v_1')+\delta(v_2')$. Since $\nu$ is a $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism, and $v_i'$ are images of suffixes of length $|v_l|-t$ of $v_l$ under elements of $\mathcal{N}$, there exists a constant $C>0$ such that $\delta(v_i')\le C_1\delta(v_l)$. 

Since $\xi_1\in\mathcal{T}_{v_1}\subset\mathcal{T}_{v_1'}$ and $\xi_2\in\mathcal{T}_{v_m}\subset\mathcal{T}_{v_m'}$, the points $\xi_1, \xi_2$ can be represented by left-infinite sequences with suffixes $v_1'$ and $v_m'$, respectively. Since they are images of each other under the action of elements of the nucleus, $\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)\ge\nu(v_1')-C$ for some constant $C_2\ge 0$.


The mass of the original chain $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ is greater or equal to $\delta(v_l)\ge C_1^{-1}(\delta(v_1')+\delta(v_2'))\ge C_1\delta(v_1')\ge C_3e^{-\ell_\nu(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$, which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:geodesicsinSigmaphi}
A geodesic path in $\Sigma_\phi$ can not have more than two consecutive horizontal edges, and it has all descending edges appearing before all the ascending ones
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Consider a horizontal path of length $kM$ starting in a vertex $xv\in\mathsf{X}^*$ for $x\in\mathsf{X}$ and corresponding to the word $s_k\cdots s_2s_1$ of elements of $\mathcal{N}$. Then $v$ and $(s_k\cdots s_2s_1)|_x(v)$ can be connected by a horizontal path $\gamma$ of combinatorial length at most $\lceil k/2\rceil$. If $k>1$, then $\lceil k/2\rceil\le k-1$. Then the path consisting of the descending edge $(xv, v)$, followed by the path $\gamma$ and then by the ascending edge from $(s_k\cdots s_2s_1)|_x(v)$ to $(s_k\cdots s_2s_1)(v)$ has length less than $M/2+(k-1)M+M/2=kM$, so $\gamma$ is not a geodesic path in $\Sigma_\phi$. This shows that a geodesic path in $\Sigma_\phi$ can not have two consecutive horizontal edges.

A path consisting of an ascending edge $(v, xv)$, horizontal edge $(xv, s(xv))$, and a descending edge $(s(xv), s|_x(v))$ has length $\|x\|+M+\|s(x)\|>M$. But there is a horizontal edge from $v$ to $s|_x(v)$ (or these vertices coincide), which shows that we can not have an ascending edge before a descending edge in a geodesic in $\Sigma_\phi$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
The function $\nu\colon \mathsf{X}^*\longrightarrow (0, \infty)$ is a positive $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Positivity of $\nu$ follows from the fact that $\Sigma_\phi$ is quasi-isometric to $\Sigma$. For every $g\in\mathcal{N}$ we have $|\nu(v)-\nu(g(v))|\le\|s\|=M$, by the triangle inequality, hence $\nu$ is $G$-quasi-invariant.

For every $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$, the geodesic paths from $\emptyset$ to $v$ in $\Sigma_\phi$ contains only ascending or horizontal edges, since, by Lemma~\ref{lem:geodesicsinSigmaphi}, in any geodesic path all descending edges come before the ascending ones, but there are no descending or horizontal edges starting in $\emptyset$.

Let $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$, and $\gamma$ be the geodesic paths starting in $\emptyset$ and ending in $v_1, v_2, v_1v_2$ for some $v_1, v_2\in\mathsf{X}^*$. Since all edges of these paths are ascending or horizontal, the labels read along them belong to $\mathsf{X}\cup\mathcal{N}$, and no consecutive labels belong to $\mathcal{N}$. Let $\overline w_1, \overline w_2, \overline w$ be the corresponding words in $\mathsf{X}\cup\mathcal{N}$, and let $w_1, w_2, w\in\mathfrak{B}^*$ be the corresponding products of the generators of the semigroup $\mathfrak{B}^*$. We obtain $w_1(\emptyset)=v_1, w_2(\emptyset)=v_2, w(\emptyset)=v_1v_2$. Since $\mathcal{N}^2|_\alpha=\mathcal{N}$ and no two consecutive generators in the wors $\overline w_i, \overline w$ belong to $\mathcal{N}$, we get that $w_1=v_1\cdot h_1, w_2=v_2\cdot h_2$, and $w=v_1v_2\cdot h_3$ for some $h_i\in\mathcal{N}^2$.

Let $\gamma_1'$ be the path starting in $h_1^{-1}(v_2)$ and labeled by the same labels as $\gamma_1$. Then it will end in $w_1h_1^{-1}(v_2)=v_1h_1h_1^{-1}(v_2)=v_1v_2$. Since the labels of $\gamma_1'$ and $\gamma_1$ are the same, there lengths are equal. Consequently,
\[\nu(v_1v_2)\le d(v_1v_2, h_1^{-1}(v_2))+d(h_1^{-1}(v_2), v_2)+d(v_2, \emptyset)\le \nu(v_1)+\nu(v_2)+2M.\]

Let $w_1'$ be the beginning of $\overline w$ (seen as an element of $\mathfrak{B}^*$) such that $w_1'\in\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes |v_1|}$. Let $w_2'$ be the rest of $w$, so that $w=w_1'w_2'$. Since $w=v_1v_2\cdot h_3$, and there are no two consecutive elements of $\mathcal{N}$ in $\overline w$, we have, for some $h_1'\in\mathcal{N}^2$, that $w_1'=v_1\cdot h_1'$. We have $v_1v_2\cdot h_3=v_1\cdot h_1'\cdot (h_1')^{-1}v_2\cdot h_3$. Consequently, $v_2'=(h_1')^{-1}v_2$ is a vertex of $\gamma$ splitting it into a path from $\emptyset$ to $v_2'$ labeled by $w_2'=(h_1')^{-1}v_2\cdot h_3$ and the path from $v_2'$ to $v_1v_2$ labeled by $w_1'=v_1\cdot h_1'$. The length of the first path is greater or equal to the distance from $\emptyset$ to $v_2$ minus $|v_2-(h_1')^{-1}(v_2)|\le 2M$. The length of the second path is the same as the length of the path with the same labels connecting $\emptyset$ to $w_1'(\emptyset)=v_1$, which is greater or equal to $\nu(v_1)$. Consequently,
\[\nu(v_1v_2)\ge \nu(v_2)-2M+\nu(v_1),\]
which finishes the proof that $\nu$ is a quasi-morphism.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
For any $x\in\mathsf{X}$ and $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ there exists $s\in\mathcal{N}$ such that 
\[\nu(xv)-\nu(v)\ge -\log\phi(s(x)).\]
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
If the geodesic path from $xv$ to $\emptyset$  starts with the vertical edge $(xv, v)$, then
\[\nu(xv)=-\log\phi(x)+\nu(v).\]

Suppose that it starts with a horizontal edge $(xv, s(xv))$ for some $s$. Since we can not have two consecutive horizontal edges, the next edge of the geodesic path is the vertical edge $(s(xv), s|_x(v))$, hence
\[\nu(xv)=M-\log\phi(s(x))+\nu(s|_x(v)).\]
We have a horizontal edge $(v, s|_x(v))$, hence, by triangle inequality,
\[\nu(v)\le M+\nu(s|_x(v)).\]
It follows that
\[\nu(xv)-\nu(v)\ge -\log\phi(s(x)),\]
which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
We have
    \[\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}} (G, \mathfrak{B})=\inf\{p\colon \theta_p<1\}\] and
    \[\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})\le \left(\frac 1p-\frac{\log\theta_p}{\log \mathsf{D}}\right)^{-1}<p\]
for every $p\in (1, \infty]$ such that $\theta_p<1$, where $\mathsf{D}=|\mathfrak{B}/G|$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proposition-18: body_md -->
The limit $\eta_p=\eta_p(G, \mathfrak{B})$ exists and does not depend on the choices of the generating set of $G$ or of the basis $\mathsf{X}$.  We have $\eta_\infty\ge\mathsf{D}^{-1}$. For all $0<p<q\le\infty$ we have
\[\eta_p\ge\eta_q,\qquad \mathsf{D}^{-1/p}\eta_p\le\mathsf{D}^{-1/q}\eta_q,\]
for $\mathsf{D}=|\mathfrak{B}/G|$.
<!-- end proposition-18 -->
<!-- proposition-19: body_md -->
\label{pr:etatheta}
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a contracting (not necessarily faithful) group. Then we have
\[\eta_p(G, \mathfrak{B})\le\theta_p(G, \mathfrak{B})\]
for every $p\in (1, \infty]$, and therefore,
\[\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})\le\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B}).\]
<!-- end proposition-19 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Recall that we call a path in the graph $\Gamma_n$ almost essential if it can be continued by one edge to an essential path. We say that a function is \emph{strongly admissible} if the sum of its values along any almost essential path is greater than 1.

Let $\phi_0\colon S \times\mathsf{X}^n\longrightarrow[0, \infty)$ be an $(S, \mathcal{N})$-strongly admissible function, where $S$ is a generating set of $G$.  We assume that $\mathcal{N}\subset S$.

 Consider a product $g=s_1s_2\cdots s_m$ of elements of $S$ such that $m=l(g)$. Consider the corresponding path in $\Gamma_n$ starting in $v$. It has length $\phi(g, v)=\sum_{i=1}^m \phi(s_i, s_{i+1}\cdots s_m(v))$. Split it into maximal almost essential segments (the last segment is non-essential, but not necessarily almost essential). Suppose that there are $k$ of them. Then $l(g|_v)\le k+1$. Since the $\phi$-length of each of the segments is $\ge 1$, we get that $\phi$-length of the path is at least $k\ge l(g|_v)-1$. 

Then, using the triangle inequality for the $\ell^p$-norms of the vectors
\[\vec F_i=\left(\phi(s_i, s_{i+1}\cdots s_m(v))\right)_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathsf{X}^n}\] and $\vec U=(1)_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}$, we get
\begin{multline*}\left(\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}l(g|_v)^p\right)^{1/p} \le\left(\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}(\phi(g, v)+1)^p\right)^{1/p}=\\
\left(\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\phi(s_i, s_{i+1}\cdots s_m(v))+1\right)^p\right)^{1/p}=\\
\|\vec F_1+\cdots+\vec F_m+\vec U\|_p\le\|\vec F_1\|_p+\cdot\|\vec F_m\|_p+|\mathsf{X}|^{n/p}=\\
\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\phi(s_i, v)^p\right)^{1/p}+|\mathsf{X}|^{n/p}\le l(g)\cdot\left(\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n, s\in S}\phi(s, v)^p\right)^{1/p}+|\mathsf{X}|^{n/p}.
\end{multline*}

By varying $\phi_0$, we get:
\[\limsup_{l(g)\to\infty}\frac{\left(\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}l(g|_v)^p\right)^{1/p}}{l(g)}\le CM_p(n)^{1/p},\]
where $C$ does not depend on $n$. Taking the $n$th root and passing to the limit, we get $\eta_p\le\theta_p$.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- proposition-20: body_md -->
\label{pr:sizeofportrait}
Let $p>\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$. Then there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for every $g\in G$ we have 
\[|\mathcal{L}(g)|\le Cl(g)^p.\]
<!-- end proposition-20 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
We have $\eta_p<1$. Let $\lambda\in (\eta_p, 1)$. Then there exist $R, n_0>1$ such that for all $g\in G$ such that $l(g)\ge R$ we have 
\[\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^{n_0}}l(g|_v)^p<\lambda^{n_0}l(g)^p.\]
Let $\mathcal{L}_{n_0}(A)$ be the intersection of $\mathcal{L}(g)$ with $(\mathsf{X}^{n_0})^*$. Denote by, for $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$ by $v'$ the longest prefix of $v$ of length divisible by $n_0$. Then $|v|-|v'|<n_0$, so the map $v\mapsto v'$ is $K_1$-to-one for some fixed $K_1$. The set $\mathcal{L}(g)$ is prefix-closed, hence $|\mathcal{L}(g)|\le K_1 |\mathcal{L}_{n_0}(g)|$.

Let $\mathcal{L}'_{n_0}(g)$ be the set of elements $v\in(\mathsf{X}^{n_0})^*$ such that $l(g|_v)\ge R$. Since there exists $k$ such that $g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^k$ and $g\in G$ such that $l(g)<R$, there exists $K_2$ such that  $|\mathcal{L}_{n_0}(g)|\le K_2|\mathcal{L}'_{n_0}(g)|$. Then $|\mathcal{L}(g)|\le K_1K_2|\mathcal{L}_{n_0}'(g)|$.

We have
\[\sum_{v\in\mathcal{L}'_{n_0}(g)}l(g|_v)^p\le l(g)^p+\lambda^{n_0} l(g)^p+\lambda^{2n_0}l(g)^p+\cdots=\frac{l(g)^p}{1-\lambda^{n_0}}. \]

It follows that
\[|\mathcal{L}(g)|\le K_1K_2|\mathcal{L}_{n_0}'(g)|\le\frac{K_1K_2}{1-\lambda^{n_0}} l(g)^p,\]
which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- defi-15: body_md -->
The \emph{portrait of an element $g\in G$} is the set $\mathcal{L}(g)$ together with the map $\alpha\colon\mathcal{L}(g)\longrightarrow S_{\mathsf{X}}$ mapping $v$ to the permutation induced by $g|_v$ on $\mathsf{X}$, and the map $\beta\colon vx\mapsto g|_{vx}\in\mathcal{N}$ for all leaves $v$ of the subtree $\mathcal{L}(g)\subset\mathsf{X}^*$ and all $x\in\mathsf{X}$.
<!-- end defi-15 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
The word growth of a contracting group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is bounded, for every $\epsilon>0$, above by $\exp(C n^{\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})+\epsilon})$ for some $C>0$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- example-13: body_md -->
Consider the Grigorchuk group $G=\langle a, b, c, d\rangle$ from~\cite{grigorchuk:80_en}. 
Take the generating set $\{a, b, c, d, ab, ac, ad\}$. Let $\eta$ be the real root of the polynomial $x^3+x^2+x-2$, and define the lengths of the generators, as in~\cite{bartholdi:upperbd}:
\begin{alignat*}{2}
\|a\|&=1-\eta^3, &\qquad \|b\|&=\eta^3,\\
  \|c\|&=1-\eta^2, &\qquad   \|d\|&=1-\eta.
\end{alignat*}
Then 
\begin{align*}
\|ab\|&=\|a\|+\|b\|=1,\\
\|ac\|&=\|a\|+\|c\|=\eta,\\
\|ad\|&=\|a\|+\|d\|=\eta^2.
\end{align*}
We have $ab=\sigma(a, c)$, $ac=\sigma(a, d)$, $ad=\sigma(1, b)$. We see that for each of them we have $\eta\cdot l(g)=l(g|_0)+l(g|_1)$. It follows that $\eta_1(G)\le\eta$.


Consider the substitution
\[\psi\colon ba\mapsto cadaba,\quad ca\mapsto baba,\quad da\mapsto caca,\]
see~\cite{bartholdiErschler:imbeddings}.

The wreath recursion satisfies $\psi(g)=\sigma (ga, ag)$ or $\psi(g)=(aga, g)$, and we have $l(\psi^n(ad))\asymp (2/\eta)^n$, where $\eta\approx 0.8015$ is the root of $x^3+x^2+x-2=0$.

We get \[\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^k}l(\psi^n(ad)|_v)^p\asymp 2^k(2/\eta)^{-kp}l(\psi^{n-k}(ad))^p,\] which implies \[\eta_p\le 2^{\frac 1p-1}\eta.\]
Note that since $\eta_\infty=\theta_\infty=1/2$, we can not have equality for large $p$.


On the other hand, it is known that $\eta_1\le\eta$, see~\cite{bartholdi:upperbd}. Consequently, $\eta_p\le 2^{\frac 1p-1}\eta$ for all $p\in (0, 1]$. In particular, we get $\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\frac{\log 2}{\log 2-\log\eta}\approx 0.7674$.

We see that $\eta_p=2^{\frac 1p-1}\eta$ for all $p\in (0, 1]$ and $2^{\frac 1p-1}\eta\le\eta_p\le 2^{\frac 1p-1}$ for all $p\in (0, \infty]$. We know $\theta_p=2^{\frac 1p-1}$ in this case (see Example~\ref{ex:Grigmodulus}).
<!-- end example-13 -->
<!-- proposition-21: body_md -->
Let $A\subset\mathcal{C}$ be a finite set, and let $P_A$ be the projector
\[P_A([g])=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} [g] & \text{if $[g]\in A$,}\\
0 & \text{otherwise}\end{array}\right.\] onto the span $\mathbb{R}^A$ of $A$.

Then the spectral radius of the operator $P_AT_p\colon\mathbb{R}^A\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}^A$ is less than or equal to $\eta_p^p$.
<!-- end proposition-21 -->
<!-- example-14: body_md -->
Consider the group $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$ computed in Example~\ref{ex:basilicaimgcomput}. The generators $a$ and $b$ have infinite order, since $a^2(0w)=0b(w)$, $a^2(1w)=1b(w)$ and $b(1w)=1a(w)$. These relations also imply that
\[T_p([a])=2^{1-p}[b],\qquad T_p([b])=[a],\]
i.e., that its matrix is $\left(\begin{array}{cc} 0 & 1\\ 2^{1-p} & 0\end{array}\right)$. The spectral radius of this matrix is $2^{\frac{1-p}2}$. We get hence an estimate $\sqrt{2}^{\frac 1p-1}\le\eta_p$. On the other hand, we know from Example~\ref{ex:thetapbasilica} that $\theta_p=\sqrt{2}^{\frac 1p-1}$. Since $\eta_p\le\theta_p$, we conclude that $\eta_p=\theta_p=\sqrt{2}^{\frac 1p-1}$ for all $p\ge 1$.
<!-- end example-14 -->
<!-- defi-16: body_md -->
\label{def:aplim}
For $p\ge 1$, let $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})\subset C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ be the set of functions $f\colon \mathcal{X}_{G}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that
\[\sum_{v\in\mathfrak{B}^*}|f(\xi_1\otimes v)-f(\xi_2\otimes v)|^p<\infty\]
for any two points $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$.

For $p\ge 1$, let $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})\subset C(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ be the set of functions $f$ such that their lift $f\colon \mathcal{X}_{G}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ satisfies
\[\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*}|f(\xi_1\otimes v)-f(\xi_2\otimes v)|^p<\infty\]
for all $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$.

For $p>1$ and $\lambda\ge 0$, let $\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{X}_{G})\subset C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ be the set of functions $f\in C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ such that for every pair $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$ there exists $C>1$ such that
\[\sum_{v\in\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n}}|f(\xi_1\otimes v)-f(\xi_2\otimes v)|^p\le C\lambda^n\]
for all $n\ge 1$.

For $p>1$ and $\lambda\ge 0$, let $\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{X}_{G})\subset C(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ be the set of functions $f$ such that for every pair $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$ there exists $C>1$ such that
\[\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^{\otimes n}}|f(\xi_1\otimes v)-f(\xi_2\otimes v)|^p\le C\lambda^n\]
for all $n\ge 1$.
<!-- end defi-16 -->
<!-- proposition-22: body_md -->
The sets $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G}), \mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G}), \mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{X}_{G}), \mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ are $*$-subalgebras of the corresponding  $C^*$-algebras $C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ and $C(\mathcal{J}_{G})$.

In particular, these sub-algebras are dense if and only if they separate the points (of $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ and $\mathcal{J}_{G}$, respectively).
<!-- end proposition-22 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Let us prove the statement for the set $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$. The proof of the other statement is analogous. The set $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is obviously $*$-invariant.

Denote by $\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f)$ the map $\mathfrak{B}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ given by $\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f)(v)=f(\xi_1\otimes v)-f(\xi_2\otimes v)$. Then the sum in the definition of $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is equal to the $p$-th power of the $\ell^p$-norm  $\|\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f)\|_p$.

For any $f_1, f_2\in C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$, we have 
\[\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_1+f_2)=\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_1)+\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_2),\] hence $\|\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_1+f_2)\|_p\le\|\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_1)\|_p+\|\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_2)\|_p$, so $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is closed under addition.

We also have 
\begin{multline*}\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_1f_2)(v)=f_1(\xi_1\otimes v)f_2(\xi_1\otimes v)-f_1(\xi_2\otimes v)f_2(\xi_2\otimes v)=\\ (f_1(\xi_1\otimes v)-f_1(\xi_2\otimes v))f_2(\xi_1\otimes v)+f_1(\xi_2\otimes v)(f_2(\xi_1\otimes v)-f_2(\xi_2\otimes v)),
\end{multline*} hence
\[\|\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_1f_2)\|_p\le\|f_2\|\cdot\|\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_1)\|_p+\|f_1\|\cdot\|\partial_{\xi_1, \xi_2}(f_2)\|_p,\]
where $\|f\|=\max_{\zeta\in\mathcal{X}_{G}}|f(\zeta)|$ is the $C^*$-norm on $C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$. It follows that $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is closed under multiplication. Its $*$-invariance is obvious.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-23: body_md -->
The algebra $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ is dense in $C(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ if and only if $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is dense in $C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$. The algebra $\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ is dense in $C(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ if and only if $\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is dense in $C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$.
<!-- end proposition-23 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
We identify continuous functions on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ with continuous $G$-invariant functions on $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ throughout the proof.

  Suppose that the algebra $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ is dense. Let us show that the algebra $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ separates the points.  Let $\zeta_1, \zeta_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$ be different points. Since the action of $G$ on $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ is proper, there exists a compact neighborhood $U$ of $\zeta_1$ in $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ not containing $\zeta_2$ such that for every $g\in G$ we have either $U\cdot g=U$ and $\zeta_1\cdot g=\zeta_1$ or $U\cdot g\cap U=\emptyset$. Moreover, the set of elements $g\in G$ satisfying the first condition is equal to the stabilizer $G_{\zeta_1}$ of $\zeta_1$, and hence is finite. 
  
  
Since $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ is dense, there exits a $G$-invariant function $\tilde f\in\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ such that $\tilde f(\zeta_1)=1$ and $|\tilde f(\zeta)|\le 1/2$ for $\zeta\notin U$. Composing $\tilde f$ with a Lipschitz function $\mathbb{C}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ equal to $1$ on a neighborhood of $1$ and to 0 for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$ such that $|z|\le 1/2$, we will get an element $f\in\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ supported in the interior of $U$ and such that $f(\zeta_1)=1$.

Since the sets $U\cdot g$ are disjoint or coincide, and $f$ is supported it their union, the function
\[h(\zeta)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} f(\zeta) & \text{if $\zeta\in U$,}\\
0 & \text{otherwise}\end{array}\right.\] is continuous. It is compactly supported, hence is contained in $C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$.
  
Let $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$ be arbitrary points. The distance between $\xi_1\otimes v$ and $\xi_2\otimes v$ uniformly on $v$ converges to 0 as the length of $v$ goes to infinity.

Consequently, there exists $n$ such that for every $v\in\mathfrak{B}^*$ with $|v|>n$ the following two conditions hold.  If $\xi_1\otimes v$ belongs to the support of $h$, then $\xi_2\otimes v\in U$, and if $\xi_2\otimes v$ belongs to the support of $h$, then $\xi_1\otimes v\in U$. 

Then, for all $v\in\mathfrak{B}^*$, $|v|>n$, we have either $h(\xi_1\otimes v)=h(\xi_2\otimes v)=0$, or $h(\xi_1\otimes v)=f(\xi_1\otimes v)$ and $h(\xi_2\otimes v)=f(\xi_2\otimes v)$. Note that the latter case happens only for at most $|G_{\zeta_1}|$ points in the right $G$-orbit of a given $v$.

It follows that $\sum_{v\in\mathfrak{B}^*, |v|\ge n}|h(\xi_1\otimes v)-h(\xi_2\otimes v)|^p\le |G_{\zeta_1}|\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^*, |v|\ge n}|f(\xi_1\otimes v)-f(\xi_2\otimes v)|^p$, which implies that $h\in\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ if $f\in\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$. We have $h(\zeta_1)=1$ and $h(\zeta_2)=0$, so we have shown that $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ separates the points of $\mathcal{X}_{G}$.
  
Suppose now that $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is dense. 
Let $\zeta_1, \zeta_2$ be two points of $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ that have different images in $\mathcal{J}_{G}$. Let $U$ be defined for $\zeta_1$ in the same way as above with additional condition that $\zeta_2\notin U\cdot g$ for every $g\in G$. We can achieve this by choosing $U$ small enough, as the images of $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ in $\mathcal{J}_{G}=\mathcal{X}_{G}/G$ are different, and the action of $G$ on $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ is proper. 

By the same argument as above, there exists a real-valued function $h\in\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ supported in $U$ and such that $h(\zeta_1)=1$.

Define then $f(\zeta)=|G_{\zeta_1}|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}h(\zeta\cdot g)$. Then $f$ is a $G$-invariant continuous function supported in $U\cdot G$ and satisfying $f(\zeta_1)=1$, $f(\zeta_2)=0$. It follows directly from the condition $h\in\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ that $f\in\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{th:DpDlambda}
The conformal dimension $\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is equal to the infimum of values of $p$ for which $\mathcal{D}_p(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ is dense in $C(\mathcal{J}_{G})$.

Moreover, for every $p>\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ the infimum of the values $\lambda$ for which $\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ is dense in $C(\mathcal{J}_{G})$ is equal to $\theta_p$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proposition-24: body_md -->
If there exists a metric $d\in\mathcal{AR}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ of Hausdorff dimension $p_0$, then for every $p>p_0$ and $\lambda\in (\theta_p, 1)$ the algebra $\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ is dense in $C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$.
<!-- end proposition-24 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
We may assume that $d$ is a visual metric associated with a $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism $(\mathsf{X}^n)^*\longrightarrow[0, \infty)$, by Theorem~\ref{th:modulus}.

Let us show that there exists $\lambda\in (\theta_p, 1)$ such that every function $f\colon \mathcal{X}_{G}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ which is Lipschitz with respect to the metric $d$ belongs to $\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda}$.

Let $L$ be the Lipschitz constant for $f$. Let $\xi_1, \xi_2\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$. We will denote by $P(\xi)$ the image in $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ of a point $\xi\in\mathcal{X}_{G}$.

There exists $n_0$ such that $\xi_i\otimes v\in\mathcal{T}\cdot\mathcal{N}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^*$, $|v|\ge n_0$, $i=1, 2$. Then, for all $v_1\in\mathsf{X}^{n_0}$ and $v_2\in\mathsf{X}^*$ we have $P(\xi_i\otimes v_1v_2)\in\mathcal{T}_{s_i(v_2)}$ for some $s_i\in\mathcal{N}$. It follows that $d(P(\xi_1\otimes v_1v_2)-P(\xi_2\otimes v_1v_2))$ is not greater than diameter of the set $\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal{N}}\mathcal{T}_{s(v_2)}$. Since each set $\mathcal{T}_{s(v)}$ intersects $\mathcal{T}_v$, the diameter of $\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal{N}}\mathcal{T}_{s(v_2)}$ is less than a constant times the diameter of $\mathcal{T}_{v_2}$, since $d$ is associated with a $G$-quasi-invariant quasi-morphism.

Using Proposition~\ref{pr:diamoftiles}, we see that for some constants $C_1, C_2, C_3$, and $\lambda\in (0, 1)$, not depending on $n$, $v_1\in\mathsf{X}^{n_0}$ and $v_2\in\mathsf{X}^n$, we have
\begin{multline*}
|f(P(\xi_1\otimes v_1v_2))-f(P(\xi_2\otimes v_1v_2))|^p\le\\
 L^pd(P(\xi_1\otimes v), P(\xi_2\otimes v))^p\le C_1\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}_{v_2})^p\le \\ C_2\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}_{v_2})^{p-p_0}\mu(\mathcal{T}_{v_2})\le C_3\lambda^{n(p-p_0)}\mu(\mathcal{T}_{v_2}),
 \end{multline*} where $\mu$ is the corresponding measure on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$.
 
 It follows that for all $n\ge n_0$ we have
 \begin{multline*}\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}|f(P(\xi_1\otimes v))-f(P(\xi_2\otimes v))|^p\le\\ 
 (\deg\mathfrak{B})^{n_0}C_3\lambda^{(n-n_0)(p-p_0)}\sum_{v_2\in\mathsf{X}^{n-n_0}}\mu(\mathcal{T}_{v_2})\le\\
  C_4\lambda_1^n |\mathcal{N}|\mu(\mathcal{J}_{G})=C_5\lambda_1^n
  \end{multline*}
  for $\lambda_1=\lambda^{p-p_0}$. Consequently, $f\in\mathcal{D}_{p, \lambda_1}$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-25: body_md -->
\label{pr:pcgreater}
Let $\xi\in\mathcal{T}$. Consider the algebra $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{p, \xi}$  consisting of functions $f\in C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{v\in\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n}}|f(\xi\otimes v)-f(\xi\otimes g\cdot v)|^p=0$ for all $g\in G$.

If $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{p, \xi}$ is dense in $C_0(\mathcal{X}_{G})$, then there exists a metric $d\in\mathcal{AR}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ of dimension $p$.
<!-- end proposition-25 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Choose a basis $\mathsf{X}$ and let $\mathcal{N}$ be the corresponding nucleus.
Suppose that $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{p, \xi}$ is dense. This algebra is also invariant under post-compositions with Lipschitz functions, so there exists a function $f\in\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{p, \xi}$ such that $f(\xi)=1$ for every $\xi\in \mathcal{T}$ and $f(\xi)=0$ for every $\xi\in\mathcal{T}\cdot g$ for $g\in G\setminus \mathcal{N}$.

For every $n$, define then the function $\phi$ on the edges of the graph $\Gamma_n$ by \[\phi(s, v)=\left(\sum_{g\in G}|f(\xi\otimes v\cdot g)-f(\xi\otimes s\cdot v\cdot g)|^p\right)^{1/p}.\]
Then $\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n}\phi(s, v)^p=\sum_{v\cdot g\in\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n}}|f(\xi\otimes v\cdot g)-f(\xi\otimes s\cdot v\cdot g)|^p\to 0$, by the definition of $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{p, \xi}(\mathcal{X}_{G})$.

Let $(s_1, v_1), (s_2, v_2), \ldots, (s_m, v_m)$ be an edge-path in $\Gamma_n$. Here $v_{i+1}=s_i(v_i)$. Suppose that $(s_m\cdots s_2s_1)|_{v_1}\notin\mathcal{N}$. Consider the corresponding sequence 
\[\xi\otimes v_1, \xi\otimes s_1\cdot v_1, \xi\otimes s_2s_1\cdot v_1, \ldots, \xi\otimes s_m\cdots s_2s_1\cdot v_1.\]
Then $\xi\otimes v_1\in\mathcal{T}$, but 
\[\xi\otimes s_m\cdots s_2s_1\cdot v_1=\xi\otimes s_m(v_m)\cdot (s_m\cdots s_2s_1)|_{v_1}\in\mathcal{T}\cdot (s_m\cdots s_2s_1)|_{v_1}.\] It follows that $f(\xi\otimes v_1)=1$ and $f(\xi\otimes s_m\cdots s_2s_1\cdot v_1)=0$. Consequently,

\begin{multline*}|f(\xi\otimes v_1)-f(\xi\otimes s_1\cdot v_1)|+|f(\xi\otimes s_2s_1\cdot v_1)-f(\xi\otimes s_3s_2s_1\cdot v_1)|+\cdots\\ +|f(\xi\otimes s_{m-1}\cdots s_1\cdot v_1)-f(\xi\otimes s_m\cdots s_1\cdot v_1)|\ge 1.
\end{multline*}
We have $\phi(s_i, v_i)=\left(\sum_{g\in G}|f(\xi\otimes v_i\cdot g)-f(\xi\otimes s_i\cdot v_i\cdot g)|^p\right)^{1/p}$. One of the summands in this sum is $|f(\xi\otimes v_i\cdot (s_{i-1}\cdots s_2s_1)|_{v_1})-f(\xi\otimes s_i\cdot v_i\cdot (s_{i-1}\cdots s_2s_1)|_{v_1})|^p=|f(\xi\otimes (s_{i-1}\cdots s_2s_1)\cdot v_1)-f(\xi\otimes (s_i\cdots s_2s_1)\cdot v_1)|^p$.
Consequently, $\phi(s_i, v_i)\ge |f(\xi\otimes (s_{i-1}\cdots s_2s_1)\cdot v_1)-f(\xi\otimes (s_i\cdots s_2s_1)\cdot v_1)|$, which implies that $\sum_{i=1}^m\phi(s_i, v_i)\ge 1$, i.e., that $\phi$ is admissible.

We conclude that $M_n(p)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$, so by Theorem~\ref{th:modulus}, there exists a metric $d\in\mathcal{AR}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ of dimension $p$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- example-15: body_md -->
Consider the Julia set $\mathcal{J}$ of $f(z)=z^2-1$, i.e., the limit space of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$. There is a topological conjugacy between the action of $f^2$ on the closure of the Fatou component containing $0$ with the action of $z^2$ on the closed unit disc. The restriction of this conjugacy to the boundary of the Fatou component can be also seen as the map induced by the morphism from the binary adding machine biset to the $\langle a\rangle$-biset generated by $\{11, 01\}\subset\mathfrak{B}_{z^2-1}^{\otimes 2}$.

Consider an arbitrary Lipschitz function on the unit circle, and transfer it to a function $\varphi$ on the boundary $B_0$ of the Fatou component of $0$ by the conjugacy. The closure of every component $C$ of $\mathcal{J}\setminus B_0$ intersects $B_0$ in a single point, so we can extend $\varphi$ to $C$ as a constant function, thus getting a continuous function on $\mathcal{J}$. The boundary $B$ of any other Fatou component of $\mathcal{J}$ is mapped onto $B_0$ homeomorphically by some iteration of $f$, so we can use that iteration to define in a similar way a copy of $\varphi$ on $B$ which is constant on the components of $\mathcal{J}\setminus B$. One can show that all such functions belong to $\mathcal{D}_{1, 1}$, and hence to $\mathcal{D}_p$ for all $p>1$. It is also easy to see that such functions generate a dense sub-algebra in $C(\mathcal{J})$. It follows that the conformal dimension of the limit space of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$ is equal to 1.
<!-- end example-15 -->
<!-- defi-17: body_md -->
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a contracting group. The \emph{uniform dimension} $\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ is the infimum of the Hausdorff dimensions of the uniform metrics on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$.
<!-- end defi-17 -->
<!-- proposition-26: body_md -->
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a contracting group. Choose a basis $\mathsf{X}\subset\mathfrak{B}$, and let $\mathcal{N}$ be the associated nucleus.

Denote by $L(n)$ the largest number for which $\mathcal{N}^{L(n)}|_v\subset\mathcal{N}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$. 

Then \[\lim_{n\to\infty}L(n)^{1/n}=\sup_n L(n)^{1/n}=\theta_\infty^{-1}.\]
<!-- end proposition-26 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
The constant function equal to $L(n)^{-1}$ on the edges of $\Gamma_n$ is admissible, since any essential path has length $\ge L(n)+1$. Consequently, $\overline M_\infty(n)\le L(n)^{-1}$. 

On the other hand, suppose that $\phi$ is an admissible function on the set of edges of $\Gamma_n$. There exists an essential path of length $L(n)+1$. Since the sum of values of $\phi$ on the edges of this path is not less than $1$, there exists an edge $e$ such that $\phi(e)\ge (L(n)+1)^{-1}$.
Consequently, $\|\phi\|_\infty\ge (L(n)+1)^{-1}$. 

We have shown that 
\[(L(n)+1)^{-1}\le \overline M_\infty(n)\le L(n)^{-1}.\]
Consequently, $\lim_{n\to\infty}L(n)^{1/n}=\theta_\infty^{-1}$. 

Consider a product of length $L(n)L(m)$ of elements of $\mathcal{N}$, write it as $g_1g_2\ldots g_{L(m)}$ for $g_i\in\mathcal{N}^{L(n)}$ and let $w=v_1v_2$ for $v_1\in\mathsf{X}^{n}$ and $v_2\in\mathsf{X}^m$. Then $g_1g_2\ldots g_{L(m)}|_{v_1}=g_1|_{g_2\cdots g_{L(m)}(v_1)}\cdots g_{L(m)}|_{v_1}\in\mathcal{N}^{L(m)}$, so $(g_1\cdots g_{L(m)})|_{v_1v_2}\in\mathcal{N}$. It follows that $L(n+m)\ge L(n)L(m)$.
Consequently, by Fekete's Lemma, $\lim_{n\to\infty}L(n)^{1/n}=\sup_n L(n)^{1/n}$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- proposition-27: body_md -->
For every contracting group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$, we have  \[\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{-\log\theta_\infty},\]
where $\mathsf{D}=|\mathfrak{B}/G|$.
<!-- end proposition-27 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Suppose that $\xi_1, \xi_2, \ldots, \xi_m$ is a sequence of points of $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ such that $\ell(\xi_i, \xi_{i+1})\ge n$. If $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m$ are suffixes of length $n$ of sequences representing points $\xi_i$, then $v_{i+1}=s_i(v_i)$ for some $s\in\mathcal{N}$. If $u_1, u_m$ are the suffixes of length $k+1$ of words representing $\xi_1, \xi_m$, then there is no element $s\in\mathcal{N}$ such that $s(u_1)=u_m$. In particular, the section of $s_{m-1}\cdots s_2s_1$ in the suffix of length $n-k$ of $u_1$ does not belong to the nucleus. It follows that $m-1>L(n-k)$. Let $\lambda>\theta_\infty$. Then $L(n)\ge\lambda^{-n}$ for all $n$ large enough, so $m>\lambda^{-(n-k)}$ for all $n-k\ge m_0$ for some fixed $m_0$. If $n-k<m_0$, then $\lambda^{-(n-k)}<\lambda^{-m_0}$, so $m>1=\lambda^{m_0}\lambda{-m_0}>\lambda^{m_0}\lambda^{-(n-k)}$. Hence $m>C\lambda^{-(n-k)}$ for all $n\ge k$, where $C=\lambda^{m_0}$.

We have shown that $-\log\lambda$ is a lower exponent for the log-scale $\ell(\cdot, \cdot)$, see Definition~\ref{def:lowerexponentforlog}. It follows that there exists a uniform metric $d(\xi_1, \xi_2)\asymp e^{\log\lambda\cdot \ell(\xi_1, \xi_2)}$ of Hausdorff dimension $\frac{\mathsf{D}}{-\log\lambda}$. Since $\lambda$ was an arbitrary number greater than $\theta_\infty$, we get \[\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})\le\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{-\log\lambda}.\]

In the other direction, suppose that $d$ is a uniform  metric on $\mathcal{J}_{G}$ of dimension $p$. Let $\delta$ be the distance in $\mathcal{X}_{G}$ (with respect to the lifted metric) from the tile $\mathcal{T}$ to the union of the tiles $\mathcal{T}\cdot g$ for $g\in G\setminus\mathcal{N}$. By definition of $L(n)$, there exists a sequence $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{L(n)+1}$ of elements of the nucleus and a word $v_0\in\mathsf{X}^n$ such that $g=(s_{L(n)+1}\cdots s_2s_1)|_{v_0}\notin\mathcal{N}$. Consider the elements $v_1=s_1\cdot v_0, v_2=s_2\cdot v_1, \ldots v_{L(n)+1}=s_{L(n)+1}\cdot v_{L(n)}$ of $\mathfrak{B}^{\otimes n}$. Then $\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i\cap \mathcal{T}\otimes v_{i+1}\ne\emptyset$ for all $i=0, \ldots, L(n)$, and  $\mathcal{T}\otimes v_{L(n)+1}\subset \mathcal{T}\cdot g$ for $g\notin\mathcal{N}$. Let $\xi_i\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i\cap \mathcal{T}\otimes v_{i+1}$. Then $d(\xi_i, \xi_{i+1})\le\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}\otimes v_i)\le\mathop{\mathrm{Diam}}(\mathcal{T}_{v_i})\asymp e^{-n\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}p}$

We have $\xi_0\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_0\subset\mathcal{T}$ and $\xi_{L(n)}\in\mathcal{T}\otimes v_{L(n)+1}\subset\mathcal{T}\cdot g$ for $g\notin\mathcal{N}$. Consequently, $d(\xi_0, \xi_{L(n)})\ge\delta$, so 
\[\delta\le d(\xi_0, \xi_{L(n)})\le\sum_{i=0}^{L(n)-1}d(\xi_i, \xi_{i+1})\le CL(n)e^{-n\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}p},\]
hence $\log\delta\le \log C+\log L(n)-n\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}p$, hence
\[p\ge \frac{n\log\mathsf{D}}{\log C-\log\delta+\log L(n)}\to\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{-\log\theta_\infty},\]
which finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- example-16: body_md -->
We have seen that, in the case of $\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1)$, we have $\eta_p=\theta_p=2^{\frac{1-p}{2p}}$ for all $p\ge 1$. It follows that $\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1))=\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1))=1$, while $\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(\mathop{\mathrm{IMG}}(z^2-1))=\frac{\log 2}{-\log 2^{1/2}}=2.$
<!-- end example-16 -->
<!-- proposition-28: body_md -->
For every contracting group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$, we have $\eta_\infty=\theta_\infty$.
<!-- end proposition-28 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Define the \emph{depth} $\rho(g)$ of $g\in G$ as the smallest $n$ such that $g|_v\in\mathcal{N}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$.

Let $\lambda>\eta_\infty$. Then there exists a finite set $A\subset G$ and $n_0$ such that $l(g|_v)\le\lambda^{n_0} l(g)$ for all $g\in G\setminus A$ and $v\in\mathsf{X}^{n_0}$. This implies that for every $g\in G$ we have
\[\rho(g)\le\frac{\log l(g)}{-\log\lambda}+C,\]
where $C$ is any number greater than $\rho(g)$ for $g\in A$.


Recall that $L(n)$ was defined as the largest number such that $\mathcal{N}^{L(n)}|_v\subset\mathcal{N}$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$. For every $n$ there exists $v_n\in\mathsf{X}^n$ and $g_n\in\mathcal{N}^{L(n)+1}$ such that $g_n|_v\notin\mathcal{N}$. Then $\rho(g_n)\ge n$ and $l(g_n)\le L(n)+1$. Therefore,
\[n\le\rho(g_n)\le\frac{\log(L(n)+1)}{-\log\lambda}+C,\] 
hence
\[L(n)\ge \lambda^{-n+C}-1,\]
for all $n$, which implies $\theta_\infty=\lim_{n\to\infty}L(n)^{-1/n}\le\lambda$. Since $\lambda$ is an arbitrary number greater than $\eta_\infty$, we get $\theta_\infty\le\eta_\infty$. But we also proved in Proposition~\ref{pr:etatheta} that $\eta_\infty\le\theta_\infty$.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:udimcdim}
The following two conditions for a contracting group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$;
\item $\theta_p=\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\theta_\infty$ for all $p\ge\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
We have $\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\theta_\infty\le 1$  if and only if $p>\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{-\log\theta_\infty}$. Consequently, if $\theta_p=\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\theta_\infty$, then $\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\frac{\log\mathsf{D}}{-\log\theta_\infty}$.

On the other hand, we have $\theta_p\le\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\theta_\infty$ for all $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ and all $p\in (0, \infty]$, by Proposition~\ref{pr:asympmodulus}. 

If there exists $p>\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$ such that $\theta_p<\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\theta_\infty$, then
\[\theta_\infty\theta_{\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})}=\mathsf{D}^{-1/\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})}\theta_{\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})}\le \mathsf{D}^{-1/p}\theta_p<\theta_\infty,\]
hence $\theta_{\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})}<1$, which implies that $\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})<\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- proposition-29: body_md -->
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a contracting self-similar group. The following conditions are equivalent.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
\item $\eta_p=\mathsf{D}^{\frac 1p}\eta_\infty$ for all $p>\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-29 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
The proof is the same as for Corollary~\ref{cor:udimcdim}.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proposition-30: body_md -->
Let $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ be a level-transitive self-similar group, $\mathsf{D}=\deg\mathfrak{B}$, and let $H\le G$ be an infinite self-similar subgroup of $G$ contained in the center of $G$. Then for every $p>0$ we have
\[\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\eta_\infty(H)=\eta_p(H)\le\eta_p(G).\]

In particular, if $\eta_\infty(H)=\eta_\infty(G)$, then 
\[\eta_p(G)=\theta_p(G)=\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\eta_\infty(G)\]
 and $\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
<!-- end proposition-30 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The inequality $\eta_p(H)\le\eta_p(G)$ is obvious, so it is enough to prove the equality $\eta_p(H)=\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\eta_\infty(H)$.
Let $\mathsf{X}\subset\mathfrak{B}$ be a basis such that $H$ is self-similar with respect to it. Take $n\ge 1$, choose $v_0\in\mathsf{X}^n$, and choose elements $r_v, t_v\in G$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$ such that $v=r_v\cdot v_0\cdot t_v$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$.

Let $h\in H$. Then
\[h\cdot v=h\cdot r_v\cdot v_0\cdot t_v=r_v\cdot h(v)\cdot v_0\cdot h|_{v_0}\]
for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$. It follows that $l(h|_v)\doteq_C l(h|_{v_0})$ for all $v\in\mathsf{X}^n$, where $C$ does not depend on $h$ (but may depend on other choices). Consequently, using the triangle inequality for the $p$-norm, when $p\ge 1$, we get that the limit
\[\limsup_{l(h)\to\infty, h\in H}\frac{\left(\sum_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n} l(h|_v)^p\right)^{1/p}}{l(h)}=\limsup_{l(h)\to\infty, h\in H}\frac{(\deg\mathfrak{B})^{n/p}l(h|_{v_0})}{l(h)}\]
does not depend on $p$. For $p\in (0, 1)$ we get the same equality, using the triangle inequality for the sum of $p$th powers. We also get
\[\limsup_{l(h)\to\infty, h\in H}\frac{\max_{v\in\mathsf{X}^n} l(h|_v)}{l(h)}=\limsup_{l(h)\to\infty, h\in H}\frac{l(h|_{v_0})}{l(h)}.\]
Taking the $n$-th root and passing to the limit as $n\to\infty$, we get $\eta_p(H)=(\deg\mathfrak{B})^{1/p}\eta_\infty(H)$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
For every contracting level transitive abelian group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$ we have
\[\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\mathop{\mathrm{c.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B}).\]
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- defi-18: body_md -->
We say that $H$ is \emph{undistorted} if there exists $C>1$ such that $l_H(h)\le Cl_G(h)$ for all $h\in H$.
<!-- end defi-18 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
If $H\le G$ is an undistorted self-similar subgroup, then $\eta_p(H)\le\eta_p(G)$ for all $p\in (0, \infty]$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{th:undistorted}
Let $(G_0, \mathfrak{B}_0)$ be an undistorted self-similar subgroup of a contracting group $(G, \mathfrak{B})$. If $\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G_0, \mathfrak{B}_0)=\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G_0, \mathfrak{B}_0)$
and $\eta_\infty(G_0, \mathfrak{B}_0)=\eta_\infty(G, \mathfrak{B})$, then 
  $\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
For $\mathsf{D}=|\mathfrak{B}/G|$ and every $p>1$, we have
\[\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\eta_\infty(G, \mathfrak{B})\ge \eta_p(G, \mathfrak{B})\ge\eta_p(G_0, \mathfrak{B}_0)=\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\eta_\infty(G_0, \mathfrak{B}_0)=\mathsf{D}^{1/p}\eta_\infty(G, \mathfrak{B}),\]
so we have equalities, which implies that $\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})=\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G, \mathfrak{B})$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-31: body_md -->
Let $(G_i, \mathfrak{B}_i)$, for $i=1, 2$, be contracting groups such that $\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G_1, \mathfrak{B}_1)=\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G_1, \mathfrak{B}_1)$ and $\eta_\infty(G_1, \mathfrak{B}_1)\ge\eta_\infty(G_2, \mathfrak{B}_2)$. Denote $\mathsf{D}_i=|\mathfrak{B}_i/G_i|$. Then \[\mathop{\mathrm{l.dim}}(G_1\times G_2, \mathfrak{B}_1\times\mathfrak{B}_2)=\mathop{\mathrm{u.dim}}(G_1\times G_2, \mathfrak{B}_1\times\mathfrak{B}_2)=\frac{\log(\mathsf{D}_1\mathsf{D}_2)}{-\log\eta_\infty(G_1, \mathfrak{B}_1)}.\]
<!-- end proposition-31 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
It follows from the definitions that 
\[\eta_\infty(G_1\times G_2, \mathfrak{B}_1\times\mathfrak{B}_2)=\max(\eta_\infty(G_1, \mathfrak{B}_1), \eta_\infty(G_2, \mathfrak{B}_2)).\]
Consequently, if $\eta_\infty(G_1, \mathfrak{B}_1)\ge\eta_\infty(G_2, \mathfrak{B}_2)$, then we can apply Theorem~\ref{th:undistorted}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
